translations.text: My king is the king of noble heaven, without pride, without contention, who created the world with its kindreds [?]; my king ever-living, ever-victorious.
King above the elements, beyond the sun; king above the depths of the ocean; king in south, north, west and east, against whom no contention is made.
King of the mysteries, who was and is, before the elements, before the ages; king ever-living still, fair of face; king without beginning, without end.
King who made the bright heaven, not proud, not unstable [?], and the earth, covered with hills, equally mighty, equally steadfast, equally strong.
King who made the noble light and the darkness with its [?]: the one is full day, the other is complete night.
King who formed, from the [?] of God, the first matter of the elements, [?] to which is likened, everlasting, the wondrous, formless mass.
King who fashioned the form of every element, who established them without [?], fair mysteries, both smooth and rough in colour, both dead and living.
King who cut out, renowned and mighty, from the first beautiful matter, the heavy earth [?], a true sound [?], whose ground is firmly founded and broad-based.
King who shaped, no narrow fold, within the circuit of the firmament, the shapely world, a certain throng [?], like a fine, truly round apple.
King who afterwards fashioned the clouds [?], surely, around the earth, a course of great skill [?] above the world, a bright victory, and the cold, watery air.
King who sifted the splendid, cold water over [?] the great cliffs [?], along the channels [?] of streams, in measures of fair measuring [?].
King who ordained eight winds [?], without fault, full of beauty: four chief winds he holds, and four fierce lesser winds.
Four other lesser winds, learned authors say; this is the truly correct number of the winds: twelve winds.
King who fashioned the colours of the winds, who established them [?], full of beauty, according to [?] customs [?], with mixtures of every varied colour.
The white, the clear purple, the blue, the very great green, the yellow, the red, certainly bold; no anger seizes them at their meetings.
The black, the grey, the speckled, the dark, the hard [?] dusky, the dun: dark colours, they are not bright or easily [?] taken.
King who ordained above every plain the eight fierce lesser winds; he fashioned without [?], a protection from trouble, the boundaries of the four chief winds.
From the east the clear, pure purple; from the south the bright, wondrous white; from the north the stormy, harsh black; from the west the [?] dun.
The red and the yellow together, between the white and the purple; the green, the blue, [?], between the dun and the bright white.
The grey, the dusky, [?], between the dun and the jet-black; the dark and the speckled in the east, between the black and the purple.
Rightly was their form arranged, their ordering was made, under [?] bolts without concealment [?], according to positions, according to placements.
The twelve winds, [?] of strife, east and west, north and south, the King who holds them harmonised them; he bound them under seven bolts.
King who distributed them by positions around the earth with many bolts: every two winds of them around a bright bolt, and one bolt over them all.
King who gave them, according to bolts, a custom, according to habits without transgression: at one time smooth after smoothness, at another time stormy.
King who [?] the measure of the slope [?] from the earth to the firmament, by which is measured the size of [?], against which the earths [?].
He set seven stars in their course from the firmament to the earth: Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, Sol, Venus, and the full-fair Moon.
The King reckoned (royal is the fame) from the earth to the moon one hundred and twenty-six thousand [miles], which they measure in its pure extent.
That is the cold air with its many streams [?] for moving, whose name, truly certain, is 'triallach' [?], the cloudy [?], pleasant [?] heaven.
Beyond that, from the moon to the sun, the King reckoned with clear, pure brightness two hundred thousand (great is the ordinance), with three [?] [and] forty-four [thousand?].
That is the noble ether, without wind, without very clear air [?], whose name, without dumb fame, is the wondrous ethereal heaven.
Three times that measure (this is clear) is the distance between the firmament and the sun. The great King of the mighty stars knew this, and He granted it to the reckoners.
That is perfect Olympus, without disturbance, without motion, according to the noble tradition of the elders of old, whose name is the third holy heaven.
Twelve thousand (a clear division) and fifteen hundred thousand: that is the fair course of the star-runner [?] from the firmament to the earth.
The measure of the spaces (a definite rush [?]) from the earth to the firmament is the same measure, in ordered ranks [?], as from the firmament to the kingdom of heaven.
That is twenty-four thousand and thirty hundred thousand miles from here to the kingdom of heaven, a great course, apart from the firmament.
The measure of all those spaces from the earth to the royal seat is the same as from the firm earth down to the depths of Hell.
The King of every lordly [?] tower [?], swift, red [?], Himself shaped the firmament; as was certain to Him, out of every plain [?] He formed it from the formless mass.
The King of all the splendid elements, [?] famous, ever-great, the great glorious one with fair hail [?], divided it into five zones.
The fifth zone, which scorches skin (the great King who runs through it [?]), against which [?] populous settlement [?] [?]; two cold zones around two temperate ones.
A cold zone in the south and a cold zone in the north; the two temperate zones (it is a great triumph); and the hot zone, it is certain, lies between the two temperate ones.
The King who provided [?] for every bright overlord, who set ordinances under obedience, made without clear [?] [?] the first form of the firmament.
As the shell is around the egg, except that [?] in lines of many [?] [?], so is the veil of the firmament around the world, through ages of ages, on its eternal course.
Its measure is cast all around [?], after a pleasant course with lasting light; harder is the estimate of what it holds [?]; it is not measured across through it [?].
It was divided according to fitting understanding, as the authors have set it out, into twelve fair sections [?] under [?] [?], twelve parts facing one another.
Each part is a month's journey for the sun, according to the knowledge of the lofty authors; on its course [?] [?], clear and bright, it goes around them every year.
In the clear firmament are seventy-two windows, which shine toward God [?] together, six windows for each part.
By the mystery of the bright King, who shaped man [?] under obedience, there are close-fitting [?] shutters, without slow delay [?], on every window.
A strong, sure cloak, a splendid [?] [?], a killing of frosts [?], fair and complete, a covering of increase [?]: He stretched it around the earth with the seas surrounding it.
Around three heavens there are [?] three heavens around it; they are complete [?]. The seventh heaven is the one that was set between the heavens.
It is not a fixed, pleasant resting place for the host of angels, but a right, fair and firm circuit, like a mill-wheel in motion, through the ages in eternal turning.
The firmament, a multitude of regions [?], and the seven noble stars that are on one course, pure and bright, since the hour they were created.
The King who divided the red-coloured [?] above the slope [?], no weak structure, the firmament, in rows, in likenesses [?], in smooth ranks, into twelve fixed divisions.
The King over every host, over every summit [?], gave a name to each single sign; [?] according to the law of rights, to the twelve divisions.
The form of each sign, a bright course, around the firmament, as the noble ones have established them ... [?]; it is from their shapes that they are named.
Aquarius, Pisces, Aries, Taurus the dwelling [?], fitting Gemini, and Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, destructive Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn.
The King who with [?] arranged them in their great masses, the row of the mountains [?] over every boundary, along which the sun and moon run.
Thirty days, a sufficient account, ten hours and a half-hour, with a journey of a third [?] over each point [?]: so long the sun runs in each sign.
The pleasant sun, according to the order of a rule, on the circuit of every year, on the fifteenth of the kalends, a fair fact, it is then that it enters each sign.
The sun in Aquarius, it is without fail [?], was made [?] in the month of January, and in Pisces ... [?], clearly it is reckoned, in the month of February.
The sun in Aries, famous is it, is shown in the month of March, and in Taurus the sun, at its will, shines in the month of April.
The sun in Gemini in the month of May, it is certain, it is no mistake; gently it warms every dwelling in the month of June, the sun in Cancer.
In the month of July the sun is in Leo; it is then that its full battle [heat] pours forth. The sun goes swiftly [?] towards its [?] into Virgo in August.
The sun shines before every throng in September in Libra; the sun hides itself [?], it does not reveal itself [?], in Scorpio in the month of October.
In Sagittarius the sun [?] them over every path in November; in December, it is a far-spread [?] fame, the sun will be in Capricorn.
Those are the signs that the Lord set upon the bright [heaven]; over every path they run around the world; the sun runs its full course along them.
Five things each day, to be known without deceit, are required of every intelligent person, of everyone without blemish of appearance who is in the orders of the church:
the day of the solar month, the age of the moon, the course of the sea [the tide] without error, the day of the week, the feasts of the pure saints, to be discussed with exact clarity.
The King who arranged them, with smooth [?] [?], with the courses of the paths of the stars; as He fixed [?] them over the divisions, He named them with swift [?] names.
Though dear to us is the half of the firmament of many stars that is before us, the other half, a festival without fetters [?], I [?] do not see it, though we might be able [?].
The King who made the [?] without rust along the track of the firmament; equally near is the sight of its face around the earth to each half.
The King who shaped the true firmament with its stars, without contempt [?], around the earth, clearly, without falsehood; it turns from one hour to the next.
The King who made a great sea-pool above the whole firmament; the other sea-pool is the sea that surrounds the earth.
The bright King whom every prophet foretold, Lord of the building of every fair grade, who set the sun of clear form, which lights the heavens around the earth.
The King who made the splendid moon and the whole sea; the King bound them under rule, so that they are fitting and harmonious.
A sixth part of the world in every direction is the size of the moon, and in the sun, clearly, is sixteen times the size of the earth.
The King who made the many thousands of creatures of the great, boundless ocean: no one knows, except my King, their names or their number.
The King who made streams of hosts of birds to fly about, of wild creatures on the mountains, of herds on the level plains.
Many are their glorious kinds, and very great their varied forms; there is no heart that could reckon that, except the King from holy heaven.
The King who made the cold air, and the bright, very red fire, and the renowned, great earth, and the very pure, swift-running stream.
The King who afterwards sowed the earth with plants and with woods: the world is full of their fragrance, with the abundance of their many fruits.
The King who rules cold and heat, my righteous King, for my true benefit [?]; it is he who established every course [?], a King beyond counting, beyond telling.
The bright King, who has not grown weary [?] of showing us every wonder, so that through them we may understand, from the bright one [?], and test [?] his miracles.
The King who made every element separately, visible and invisible; except the King who shaped them, there is no such king upon earth.
There is no one among mighty men, among angels or archangels, who has understood through his searching [?] the wonders that belong to my King, my great King, the King of noble heaven.
The King who made bright heaven, with its borders at his command: a choice, song-filled, fortified dwelling of the wonderful host of archangels.
Heaven with its many throngs, noble, peaceful, not narrow; a firm, great city with [?]; the world is but a tenth of its size.
There are there three walls without fault that surround heaven: a wall of pure green, fair work, a wall of gold, a wall of purple.
The green wall, without gloom, on the outside; the golden wall next to the surface of the city; within, beside the fair bright glory, a very great wall of pure purple.
There is there, I declare [?], a bounded city, equally broad; there are in it, toward which light spreads [?], a long way, four chief doors.
The size of each door separately of the four chief doors, side to side, by measurement afterwards [?]: a thousand [paces] across each single door.
There is a cross of gold in each door, which a host of everlasting light beholds [?]; the King shaped them without [?]; they are thick and very lofty.
A bird of red gold on each cross, above, of great glory, not unknown [?]; in each cross, for [?], a very great precious gem of bright stone.
An archangel each day, dear proclamation, with his host from the King of heaven, with choral song, with clear music, around each single cross.
There is there a green before each door, fair in its exact measure; I liken each of them in excellence to the earth with its seas.
The circuit of each green separately, with its silver sunny places [?], with its excellent flowery borders, with its glittering plants.
Though it may seem vast to you, bright company, the size of the spacious greens, a wall of silver, without any work of decay, was made around each single green.
The outer enclosures of the walls outside around the fortress on every side, with whole, peaceful dwellings for [?] of many thousands.
Eight enclosures there in order, which meet around the city: the venerable paths are no match [?] for the size that is in each enclosure.
Each enclosure full of plants, with its bronze sunny places [?]; a wall of fair, firmly packed clay [?] stands strongly around each enclosure.
Ten walls, clear the boundary, in their enclosures and their greens, besides the three walls outside that are around the chief city.
There are forty doors in the dwelling of heaven, with its royal seats: three to each smooth [?] lawn, and three to each enclosure.
There are four doors in front, facing out from the outer enclosures, toward the [?], with floods [?] of rules, toward the same approach [?].
A door-leaf of silver, a fair adornment, for every door of that lawn; door-leaves of bronze, gracefully made, for the doors of the enclosures.
The walls of all the enclosures, from the fortress outward, are likened to [?] from the earth to the moon.
The wall of the lawn, as is fitting, was made of white bronze; its height, vast in its splendour, reaches from the earth to the bright sun.
The three walls, great their [?], surround the chief city; they show their height, without rust, from the earth to the firmament.
The walls are set outward around the fortress, around the city; each wall has its gracious course, bright work, each clearly distinct [?] from the other.
The King who established with his might the stations around the chief city: certain are the dwellings from the fortress outward, in the lawns and in the enclosures.
The hosts of Adam's seed, a great feat, in their divisions according to their certain judgement [?]; clearly, by law, each of them has reached past [?] the place of every station.
Each host of them will be apart in the enclosures and in the lawns, with full rights according to their merit, with peace and with prosperity.
The saints in new [?], with grace, under victorious [?], after the battle of [?]: they are separated from the host outside and borne into the great city.
The city of God with its light: though great are its chief doors, none go into it from the dwelling of earth except only three kinds of people.
A person who fulfils God's law; a person who is truly a virgin; and, with an act of confession not hidden, a wonderful person of repentance.
The saints outside are summoned together into the chief city—excellent for them, a renowned festival—each of them through the chief door.
The beautifully formed doors, pure and gleaming, of precious stone, with great renown, which hosts approach [?], with door-leaves of red gold.
Three approaches [?] to each door, fair, pure, [?], measured along the side; to each stone course [?], a keen path; an approach [?] on each single wall.
The bridges [?] of the perfect doors, a fair, bright path of red gold; they are full of lustre, bright steps [?], each step higher than the other.
From step to step, a keen path, the climb into the chief fortress is smooth; a fair, peaceful host, a path that reaches it, many thousands of hundreds of hundreds.
Around the walls, great wealth [?], in the middle of the chief city, are bright, glassy, radiant terraces [?] and strong bridges of red gold.
There are flowering lands there, ever fresh at every season for ever, with fruits of every beloved fruit, with honey-sweet scents.
There is comfort there without sorrow [?]; there is light without extinguishing; there is music, clear, fair, pleasant, lasting, loving, and smoothly sweet.
There is that which satisfies every host in the very great royal kingdom: the sound of the ranks [?], the bright music, the scent of the fragrant flowers.
There are many dwellings [?], noble and whole; there are many steady, modest choirs; there are many hosts there, a polished [?] course; there is much music from every single choir.
There are broad pools there, beautiful their contents [?], holy and [?]; bright, around them choirs sing, joyful, blessed, sweet-tasting.
There are slender streams there of every kind of pleasant liquid, by which hosts are refreshed [?], ever [?]; there are many white wells there.
There are abundant flagstones [?] there; there are very golden seats; [?] the hosts that have taken them; there are many royal streams there.
There are many great trees of the land there, many lands to choose among, many treasures upon treasures [?], whole and distinct; many hundreds upon hundreds of level plains.
There is much music of a fair choir without sin in the one plain [?] of starry heaven; many a joyful [?] course, many a series of melodies, beyond counting or telling.
There are, after that, in ranks of rule, a hundred and four and forty, before the face of the King who holds them, according to the reckoning of their rewards.
From the beginning of the world until Doom the children of Adam, whatever their speech, could not, however great the toil [?], tell each single one of their rewards.
Besides those that they hold, there are in heaven as many rewards as the drops of rain, a swift sound [?], or the flakes of snow that fall.
The perfect throne of the great gracious King is in the midst of the chief city; many hundreds of thousands surround it round about its base [?].
Of red gold the whole royal throne was made for the King of Heaven: a King with crowns who has set it [?] above golden walls.
Angels with lights stand nearest to the chief doors; Archangels with their hosts are nearest to the holy angels.
The Virtues, the strength of every plain [?], are nearest to the Archangels; the Powers, a divine strength, are nearest to the Virtues.
The Principalities, smooth their wisdom, are nearest to the Powers; the Dominations, a firm throng, are beneath the [?] of the platform [?].
Wondrous is the whole host that has stepped onto the step [?] of the royal throne: holy is the great King who has supported the Thrones with their great throngs.
The hosts of Cherubim have set themselves round about the royal throne; above, beyond each one, under the bright King, the noble host of Seraphim are ranged.
The nine orders of heaven, holy their state, are around the King of all matter, without defeat [?] against strength [?], without boasting [?], without envy.
With full [?] before the King of law [?], this is their exact number: two [?] and sixty-six [?], a host in excellence, each single order of the orders.
The number of each host, a festival without failing: there is no one who could know it, except that the King knows it, who created them out of nothing.
A noble King above them all, King of Heaven with [?], an excellent, righteous, steadfast King, a royally generous King on his royal throne.
A very young King, a King old from long ago, a King who shaped heaven around the pure sun, King of all things, holy with grace, a fair King, a gentle King, a shapely King.
A King who made a pure heavenly house for angels, without wandering [?]: the land of the saints, of the sons of life, a fair plain, long and broad.
He arranged a throne, a noble peace, steadfast before the King's [?] path; a fair circuit, pure, bounded, bright, for the wondrous folk of repentance.
A great King, around whom over the host resounds 'Holy Lord of Sabaoth', which they sing on high [?], a course of love, the song of the four and twenty fair saints.
A King who ordained the true choir of the four and twenty fair saints; beautifully they sing a chant for the host: 'Holy God of Sabaoth.'
A steadfast, generous, excellent, fair King, peace, throne, possession, noble treasure, with whom is the flock of lambs, a bright cry, around the great pure, unblemished Lamb.
The bright King who set the Lamb upon the mountain I am speaking of [?], with four thousands of sons following it, forty and a hundred, a pure company.
A bounded [?] choir, with glories of form, of the youths without defilement; together they sing pure music following the radiant Lamb.
Equally fair, equally swift, bright, on the mountain following the Lamb, with written on their faces, with grace, their name and the name of the Father.
The King who ordained the voice from the heavenly ones for sounding [?]: broad, fierce, keen, of bright strength [?], like the wave-roar of many waters.
Or like the sound of harps, a cry they love [?]; they sing without weariness [?], very nobly, in full throngs [?] above every tree [?]; or like the very great roar of thunder.
The King of the tree of life with its blossoming, a way to which noble rank runs [?]; its top and its spreading dew [?] have spread on every side over the great plain of heaven.
On it sits the splendid flock of birds, which holds the bright grace of perfect music, without decay, with choice grace, of fruit or of leaves.
Beautiful is the flock of birds that it holds: every bird bright and good, with a hundred feathers; they sing without fault, with bright clearness, a hundred songs from each single feather.
The King who made many splendid dwellings, many fair deeds, just and complete; with the very great King, beyond every plain, is every great order, without lack.
He has seven heavens, perfect strength, without taboo [?], without fault, fair-spoken [?], around the earth, with floods of fire, with the name of each single heaven.
Air; ether above every throng; Olympus; the firmament; the heaven of water; the heaven of perfect angels; the heaven in which is the fair, great Lord.
He has many wondrous throngs; he has many dwellings without confusion [?]; he has nine orders, with holy [?] ...; he has an abode for each single order.
There is the tenth order, which holds, without fail, the sound seed of Adam: men under [?] ... [?] until they come to the fair, bright Lord.
There is peace there, there is perfect joy, without sorrow, without reproach [?], for the hosts, stately towers; there is lasting, everlasting life.
Of what good there is with dear, mighty God for His saints in the holy house, there is no one, along the paths of knowledge, who could tell its hundredth part.
The Lord, head of every bright order, ... [?] the throng of everlasting life, may He save me after leaving my body [?] ... [?], the King who made heaven. The King who made bright heaven.
The King who created the nine orders of heaven for fair, modest fashioning [?], ... [?] of pure form, for worshipping Him, for honouring Him.
Three orders of them, pure thunder [?], that are nearest to the earth: Angels, who attend to music [?], Archangels, Virtues.
Powers, of pleasant fame, these are the three middle orders; Principalities, battle without weakness; and Dominations.
The three highest orders of them, in the presence of the high King: Thrones, for the bright royal seat, Cherubim and Seraphim.
The tenth order, it is sung by you [?], without fail, the sound seed of Adam, above the world without danger with the King, whom my holy King has raised up.
The King who arranged the orders with the measures of every good gift, with ... [?] their fair deeds, for seeking Him [?], for honouring Him.
Seven orders there, eminent their deeds, for the special ... [?] of the high King, ever for them, without ... [?] of form, through eternity, to His delight.
Two orders of them, most certain in division, to help the seed of Adam, for every customary, pure task [?]: Angels and Archangels.
Bright, pure Angels, right their deed, according to God's will for messengership; the Archangels, without fault, are the high messengers.
Virtues, strengths everywhere, for performing fair, pure miracles; Powers, shapely their garb [?], excellent for governance.
Principalities, of flowering form, they are for appointed deeds [?]; Dominations, holy of form, a noble host for ruling.
Thrones and Dominions in their might, before the royal seat of the high King: a multitude who sing bright music without ceasing, the Cherubim and Seraphim.
The choir that sings in star-fair heaven completes [its song] without fading [?]; a bright company, [?] the twenty-four fair elders.
The whole hosts answer them, and the many grades join with them, so that the host sings: "Sanctus Deus Sabaoth."
The King has revealed to me, a splendid utterance, something of the measures of the many grades: of their rich, populous stations, of their hosts, of their many virtues.
Of their appearance [?] beyond [?] the world, in ranks of many-coursed stars; their great beauty [?] the sun, so that there is nothing of equal brightness.
Of their excellence [?], of their humility, of their gentleness, of their constant harmony, of their sincere goodwill without fault, of their charity, of their mercy.
Of their wholeness, a path without doubt, of their splendour, of their radiance, of their bright, fair, pure form, of their holy, wondrous countenance.
Of their seats, of their ranks, of their courses, of their deeds, of their pure songs, of their wondrous and varied ways, of their dwellings, of their many weapons.
The number of the angels in heaven, according to the bright, fair Lord, by revelation (a sure art), after spiritual disclosure:
It is not the number, O King, of the full company under fair protection, but only the number of the host that dwells in the company of each archangel.
One, two, three for a while, two added to them so that it makes five; twice five, by bright reckonings, that is the number ten.
Twice ten sure ones, a swift thunder, go to make the certain twenty; and three tens, they bring strength, that is how they go to make thirty.
After the thirty, a living display, they add to it, O King: four tens, according to sound rules, that is the number forty.
Five tens, following a good track, that is how they go to make fifty; six tens, without [?], without [?], that is the number sixty.
Seven tens make a full seventy, eight tens a very great eighty, nine tens make ninety after that, and ten tens the pure hundred.
Ten hundreds make a thousand, a great measure, and ten thousand make a legion; ten legions, always, every day, that is how they go to make a cuneus.
Ten cunei, clearly as it is reckoned, that is how they go to make a mares; ten mares, the honour of thousands of renown, surely make a caterva.
Ten catervae, it was heard, go to make an exercitus; ten exercitus, firm indeed, go surely to make a turba.
Ten turbae, sure of the strong throngs, that is how they go to make an agmen; ten agmina of angels of bright grade are in the company of each archangel.
There are seven archangels in heaven with the King of star-bright heaven; with each archangel separately are seventy agmina of angels.
That is the ninth grade that was made in holy, noble heaven: bright, pure angels without blemish, in the companies of the archangels.
The eight grades besides that, God created them surely and firmly; but apart from the most bright King in heaven, there is no one who has counted their number.
I recount, with invocation before the King of law, the names of the twenty-four fair men, a [?] throng of the hosts of angels, of the noble ones, of the archangels:
Gabriel, Michael, good their power, Raphael, delightful Panachel, Babichel, Raguel of great fame, Mirachel, Rumel of royal custom.
Fafigial, sound Sumsagial, Sarmichiel, Sarachel of noble grade, Uriel, Hermichel, good and fair, Sarachel, Barachel of brilliant fame.
Lihigiel; Darachiel, without blemish; Segiel; with Sariel, very strong; Lonachiel; Arachiel then [?]; Stichiel; Gallichiel, clear and pure.
Let us pray to them, a sure protection without failing, to the King who shaped heaven, for my life without sorrow [?], a fair form, through eternity in eternal union.
Whoever recites the portion of the nine grades between matins and the final hour [?] shall have heaven, a strong dwelling, in eternal union with the archangels.
A third of them, hosts that were heard of, were in heaven before the transgression; that whole third, under a painful stroke, went down to Hell.
I beseech you, O fair Lord, for my excesses, for my failings: grant me forgiveness here for my faults, for my ignorance.
Though there was ignorance on my part in reckoning the vastness of the many grades, what I have said, a lasting blessing, is in praise of my great King.
Though I had a hundred strong tongues to speak without fault, I could not declare through all eternity the hundredth part of the wonders of my high King.

The lasting high king of the speckled world numbered every host of special wisdom: their cleric, their noble [?], their abbot [?]; the noble King who created them. The King who created the nine grades.
My royal King, above every lord, said to Lucifer: 'There shall be under you, since I have made you bright, many myriads of archangels.'
'Give honour in due order to Adam, to my likeness; the nine grades of pure, clear brightness shall be subject [?] to your protection [?].'
'Honour to Adam — I do not hide it — I will not give, because I am the elder; for I was a high angel [?] before every lord, that I should subject myself to the younger one [?].'
The King of the stars, the righteous, truly fair Lord, said to him: 'You shall not have pure honour, since you do not give obedience to Adam.'
Lucifer spoke openly a proud answer of evil intent: 'I will be a bright king over every matter; the beloved [?] angels will serve me.'
'The angels shall be under my feet; I will make my own exaltation; I will be lord over every throng; there shall be no other king above me.'
Lucifer, with the number of his grade — his self-exaltation overthrew him; his harsh pride brought him down; he was driven to Hell.
A thousand years, in pure manner, the scriptures declare, from the creation of the angels, a just deed, until transgression overtook him.

The high King of the noble stars [?] surpasses the fortress [?] of the broad-faced world; not slender is his might over every region; better than every king is my royal King. My royal King above every lord.
The King made a fitting prison for Lucifer, for demons: a dark, gloomy, tearful, rough, bitter land, whose name is Hell.
A city of horror, of fierce [?] battles, without health, bitter, full of wailing, fearful, dreadful, of many judgments [?], perilous, [?], full of lamentation.
Bands of beasts, roaring of pains, spits of torment for the hosts [?]; drowning, plaguing, crushing [?], heat, ebbing [?], [?], hacking, burning.
Around the huge beast, with noisy peaks [?], with heavy waves [?], with many-headed swarms [?]: with leaves [?] of sparks against every host, with spits of very red embers.
Five hundred heads for painful rending [?], five hundred teeth in each single head, a hundred hands, a hundred palms, a grey apparatus [?], a hundred nails on each single palm.
Many black beetles, dark throngs, many slender, crooked, round worms, many sharp hounds [?], [?], cruel, many lasting red-mouthed beasts.
Many toads full of fierceness, wandering about in torment [?], around every circuit of the city, many very nimble serpents.
Many furnaces [?] of fierce [?] sea-monsters, of [?] bright-red beasts, many forms of bitter-tasting dragons [?], many fierce, swift lions.
Many fierce flames on every side, many showers of rough fire, many dense masses [?] heaped up [?], many dark black embers [?].
There is a great number of seas, alas [?], in Hell, with floods of heavy [?], for plaguing the spectral hosts, for drowning them, for tormenting them forever.
A sea of black darkness, a wretched gloom; a sea of the glow of heavy red fire; a stinking sea, a mighty sea, of dense [?] colour; a sea of clouds, a sea of serpents' venom.
The bitter sea in which the host sits, many a shape [?] under heavy wailing; in every quarter, under raging sorrow, weeping, 'Woe!', and great lamentation.
Thirst, cold and withering heat, [?] with hideous rough [?]; a swift jet-black host upon them, with yelping, with complaint.
The sharp cry of griffins, fury in anger, [?] of red tears, against their [?] without bright [?], with strong, fiery scourges.
Four times forty hundred [torments], which do not pass along a single path, exist for the damnation of the Devil in Hell of many torments.
Though there were a hundred thousand men with iron tongues, they could not, until the Judgement [?], give a sure count of a single one of those torments.
For there are more torments there, in terrible, narrow Hell, than plants on plains or leaves on woods.
There is a king there whose manner is not kingly: griffin-like, mean, with hundreds of many tricks, gloomy, base, clamorous, crooked of face, complaining, quarrelsome.
Wrathful, grim, practised in treachery, angry, cold, reproachful, dark, [?], who loves battle, swift, contentious, proud.
Violent, [?], of many plunderings, pestilent, thunderous, destructive, [?], greedy-mouthed, hideous [?], fierce, wretched [?], red [?].
A king who has brought heavy, sharp vengeance on the unclean host of Hell: wretched, thin [?], hungry, [?], pale, forever poor.
All the sufferings of the host in the gaping maw of harsh Hell, though I had a hundred swift tongues, I could not recount in my lifetime.
The dwelling of Hell, many torments: woe to whoever is long under its harsh compulsion; a mournful valley, narrow, hideous [?]; the great, most mighty King made it. The King made a fair prison.
The King made smooth Paradise, a bounded circuit, firm, evenly sloped, a fair, fruitful land, a most excellent dwelling, for men before the transgression.
The King blessed the smooth, level land of Paradise, in which he planted a noble [?], after fixing every choice [?], with an abundance of every fruit.
With full, luxuriant plants, with [?], with grassy lands, with clusters of flowers on every plain, with fragrant blossoms.
With the sweetness of fair [?] that was heard, with delight, with pleasantness, with green-topped, famous lands, [?] showing perpetual summer.
Teeming, dewy [?], rich in land, vigorous, a plump land, choice, wave-green, a noble, most excellent land, a fruitful valley, beautiful, fair, four-cornered [?], shapely.
A just, firm plain, a fortified height [?], a wall for help [?], lofty and very bright, the shelter of all, a strong wall, ever-smooth, ever-fresh, ever-fruitful.
A sound, lasting dwelling, noble peace, a firm, sustaining [?] wall, truly holy, ancient streams, [?] ranks, without decay, without lack.
A good plain, [?], with thousands of diadems [?], [?], colourful, certain [?] dwelling, with rich paths [?], with vast herds [?], with many musics.
The King ordained in its midst a well [?] full, from which come, clear of form, four ever-flowing streams.
A stream of wine, a stream of oil, a dear portion, a stream of pure-white new milk, a good stream of honey, pure work, for the nourishment of the holy souls.
Here is the name of each sound stream separately, openly, for the fame of a fair distribution: Pison, Gihon, lovely and free of sorrow, Tigris and Euphrates.
Pison flows eastward on its course; Tigris flows westward on its sound course; Euphrates, victorious, goes southward; Gihon runs northward, swift and straight.
The oil flows east by a sound track; the wine flows west in streams of constant flow; the honey flows south, of great excellence; the milk flows north-east.
They circle around and then turn back again, at the will of the King of holy heaven. They never fail or dry up, and are without [?], on every side under the borders of Paradise.
The King sent a flock of dear birds, without sorrow, [?] heaven. They sing songs without fault, lively, under the trees of Paradise.
The fair birds sing in pure harmony, unceasingly and without error, a noble path according to the rules of grace [?]: fair choirs of a hundred good melodies.
A hundred hundreds of birds in flocks, a hundred feathers, a hundred songs for the choirs: many hundreds of songs, firm and open, are sung clearly to the King of heaven.
The King shaped beautiful Paradise. It is he who [is?] our silver [?]. He set a great, strong wall around it, made of gold, all the way around.
The King of the green-topped, flourishing world, the King of Paradise with its many fruits, afterwards shaped a pair of every kind of living creature.
The King raised up noble Adam, in a form free of danger, fair and modest, with love and without harm [?]. This was famous. He was in Paradise before his expulsion.
Adam lay for three periods without warmth, as if extinguished, under pure [?], on the hard earth, without guidance, without a soul, without life.
Adam's body lay for three periods without a soul, for certain reasons, [?] without sadness: a clear sign prefiguring the resurrection of Christ.
On the third day after his creation, Adam's soul was shaped, after [?] choosing [?], before it was joined to the true body.
Afterwards he was named from the four bright stars, which God shaped for you: Arctos, Dysis, Anatole, Mesembria.
Nine full months, a dear [?] presence, passed from the time Adam received a soul until his wife was shaped, according to the account of sound, learned historians.
Her name was noble Eve: [?], radiant, fair and modest, dear, shapely, a choice portion, the excellent foundation of a true offspring.
Then Adam rose from his sleep without delay [?], and he saw the woman: gentle in colour, stately, distinguished, well-shaped.
When he looked at her face, he chose her above every [?]. He promised her, a clear course [?], that she would be the special love of many.
'Everyone, mother and father alike, will openly submit to you. From today forever, [?] victory, each one of us will be entirely at your will.'
High lords of the [?], a royal [?], fierce [?] at a fair cross [?]. The King who made Paradise watched over [?]. This was famous. The King made smooth Paradise.
The King spoke a pure address to Eve and to Adam: by God's command they were to eat the fruits of Paradise, a pledge without bond [?].
'Eat with pleasure the fruits of Paradise, of noble fragrance, many and all, in a [?] portion. All of it belongs to you except one tree.'
'You will know a life under rule, without misery, without strife, without anxiety, without toil at [?], without age, without evil, without blemish.'
'Without decay, without hard disease, in eternal life with eternal victory, you will go to heaven, a bright [?], at the choice age of thirty years.'
A thousand years, a victorious [?] cry, and six hours: without falsehood and without danger, it was heard, Adam was in Paradise.
God our helper (nobles affirm it), who shaped every fitting, complete thing: not [?] our question; the King who spoke the utterance. A King who spoke a pure utterance.
So the Devil was envious of Adam and his offspring, that they should be here without fault (a clear saying) and go in their whole bodies to heaven.
All the animals that the [?] King, my holy King, had created: outside Paradise, without [?], it was Adam who ruled them.
Whenever the hosts of the seven heavens came from every region around the High King, every fair, bodily animal would come to Adam.
Each of them would come from its place, graciously, at his summons and to pay homage to Adam. Eager was the manner in which they came to delight him.
God from heaven had laid it on all the animals that they should come from every side without urging, so that they would be before the face of Paradise.
Afterwards the unruly creatures would turn sunwise, without a seed of pride, each of them back to its dwelling, purely, after Adam had blessed them.
Fierce and keen, [?] by twenties, was the beast, very harsh, very [?], wondering how he might find a way under heaven to destroy Adam.
Lucifer, full of [?] questions, went among the animals, into the host outside Paradise, and it was there that he found the serpent.
"It is not for nothing that you are outside," said the Devil to the serpent, "with your quick shrewdness (a clear saying), with your cunning, with your sharpness.
"It was a great danger and a wrong that Adam was set over you: he is the youngest of the creatures [?]; it would be no crime for anyone to destroy him.
"Since you are more eager for battle, and were created earlier, and are more cunning than every other kind of creature, do not let the younger one subdue you.
"Take my counsel without hesitation; let us make a covenant in friendship. Listen yourself to my pure intention, and do not go to Adam [?].
"Give me a place in your body, as is my right and as my understanding requires, so that the two of us may go [?] together to Eve.
"Let us tempt her together with the fruit of the forbidden tree, so that she may then fully press the food on Adam.
"If only the two of them go together against the command of their Lord, they will have no favour with God here; they will come out of Paradise without bloom."
"What reward will I have before every assembly," said the serpent to the Devil, "for welcoming you into my fair, faultless body to dwell with me?
"For my toil for you after that in destroying Eve and Adam, and for truly going with you into the struggle, whatever deed you may fight against?"
"The reward I will give you, since our great evil is so great: our union in way of life and in fervour; we will always be named together."
Once he had found a dwelling forever, he took the form of the serpent. Slowly he came to rest beside Paradise, at the door.
The serpent called from outside: "Do you hear me, wife of Adam? Hurry, Eve of fair form, before everyone else, to speak with me."
"I have no leisure for anyone's conversation," said Eve to the serpent. "I am outside, attending to the unruly animals."
"If you are the Eve who has been heard of with fame for excellence in Paradise, Adam's beautiful, unwithered wife, it is on her that my full desire is set."
"When Adam is not here, it is I who guard Paradise. Without weariness, [?] smooth honey-drops [?], I serve the animals."
"Though Adam goes away from you, though he makes his fair round elsewhere, when he is not here at that hour, do you attend to the host in Paradise?
'He has left to me, a feast of purity, the tending of the animals, while he goes, of pure fame and unfailing [?], by himself to worship the Lord.'
'There is another thing I would ask of you,' said the slender, pleasant serpent, 'since your fair understanding is pure and dear, O Eve, O wife of Adam!'
'Whatever you have in mind to say that will not distress [?] [me], O gentle, modest creature, surely it will not be obscure; I will declare it to you here in sincerity.'
'Tell me, noble Eve, since we have come to converse: with the Prince who judges you here, is your life good in Paradise?'
'Until we go without fault, in our bodies, in due order, to heaven, we seek no lordship of the world here, [having] all the good that is in Paradise.'
'Every [?] ..., as has been heard, God has given them [to us] in Paradise, all of them openly, except one tree; that one is under a rule [of prohibition].'
'Dear God has made Paradise lawful for us, O creature white as a drop [of milk], with the abundance [?] it holds, except only the fruit of the one tree.'
'"Leave this tree untouched," he commanded me and Adam; "the fruit of a harsh tree, beyond what is permitted [?]: you would be dead if you ate of it."'
'Though you are of such great fame, you and Adam, O Eve, you are no wiser, O fair, pure one, than one of the animals.'
'Though there is a great host about you outside, it is pitiful that you have no understanding: like every brute animal, so you are, in one rank with them.'
'He has not given you full lordship, but only good alone; since he has not given you anything of evil, your understanding is the worse for it.'
'Great is your lack of wisdom; God is deceiving you, since it is from the one tree that evils break forth, and he does not let you taste anything of it.'
'For this reason the bitter tree was forbidden, and for this reason you are not let at it: so that you might not have in your understanding the distinction between good and evil.'
'Do not be timid; go to the tree to try a single apple; the distinction between good and evil you will have at once from the high Lord.'
'Though your understanding is good, bright course, though your counsel is full of grace, I dare not go to the tree, for fear of death, lest I die.'
'Come yourself, O serpent, to the tree, and bring an apple from it; only let the apple come to me, and I will divide it between me and Adam.'
'We shall know before every throng, if only we eat the apple, a tale without falsehood, bright course, whether it is true as you say.'
'O bright Eve without fetter, open the door of Paradise for me; without sorrow, if only I get inside, I will bring the apple from the tree.'
'Even if I open for you so that you go in to the tree, even if you bring an apple, there will be no staying for you here to remain in Paradise.'
'But I will give you the apple for the distinguishing of good and evil; without any fault I will go out, unless bondage or fetter holds me back.'
Eve secretly opened the door before the serpent; without any [?] it went, it was not slow; it ran up to the one tree.
Eve took the perfect apple from the branch, a most pitiful tale; Eve ate half of it, it was not pure; she left the other half for Adam.

The King who subdued the host of Hell ... [?] ... he struck them down [?] with a pitiful, harsh action [?]; the toilsome one fought through battle ... the edged [?] ...; it was envious. The Devil was envious of that.
When Eve had eaten her half of the harmful apple, her body [?] changed ... [?], and her fair covering fell from her.
Eve, faultless before that, it was a wonder to see her naked; a fit of trembling seized her, without fair form, so that she cried out to Adam.
Eve called, as was her right. Adam himself came without refusal, without fault, and saw his wife stark naked.
'I do not like the state you are in,' said Adam to his good wife. 'What has brought you into this plight? Who has violated your holy garment?'
'I will not tell you that, my lord Adam, until you quickly take from me, without bright fear [?], half of this apple.'
When Adam took, openly, half of the forbidden apple, his garment left him utterly [?], so that he himself was naked.
'Who betrayed you, foolish woman? Who persuaded you, so that you were not truly wise? You have brought us into a grievous and toilsome state; you have ruined yourself, you have made a fool of me.'
'It was truly a serpent, as has been heard, that entreated me when it came into Paradise; after coming to me here, it gave me an apple from the forbidden tree.'
'Then it said to me here: "Woman, take the apple from me if you wish to know evil, so that your understanding may not be weak."'
'"O Eve, if you wish to know the difference between good and great evil, take this fair, pure apple and share it between you and Adam."'
'So I took the apple from it, along with the offence, for I did not know what evil it was until I saw myself naked.'
'I went about west and east; I could not escape it [?]. It was not gentle; strange was the rushing of the wood [?]; it sent me under the trees of Paradise [?].'
'The serpent has defiled us, rough its form [?]; through its urging it has brought us to toil. Long ago was its fair deed determined [?]. Its lie has ruined us, O Adam.'
'O Eve, with many misdeeds [?], would that we had never seen your apple! It is plain upon us, since we are naked, that we have met with great evil.'
'Yet there is something worse that comes of it: the separation of body and soul — the body rotting in the hard earth, the soul going to Hell.'
When their garment fell from them, sorrow filled them at their meeting [?]; grievous to them was the ugliness of their bright bodies, with no pure veil to protect them.
The colour of their bodies was plain to each of them, since they were left in clear nakedness; to shelter their modesty, a bright covering [?], they took the leaves of the fig tree.
Nothing among created things was found fit to cover them except the fig tree alone, a feeble tree in gracious Paradise, unlike any tree that had abundant foliage [?].
Adam heard, at the gathering of the angels [?], the command spoken to Gabriel: 'Let a bright horn be sounded by you rightly, so that its voice may reach the seven heavens.'
'Come, all of you, in your pure ranks, to an assembly with our Creator, triumphantly, at the work of the dear fortress [?], you hosts of angels from the seven heavens.'
'Gather for a full hosting; let the assembly not be scanty, so that you may go, as has been clearly proclaimed, in the company of God to Paradise.'
Then the ruddy King went to Paradise with his great host; before him, in a firm and faultless band, went a choir of angels singing together.
He sat upon the cherubim — that truly was the royal seat of the High King — in the midst of gracious Paradise, at the place where the tree of life stands.
Every host was arranged in order, each bright rank with its company, and the great, radiant King himself sat upon the cherubim.
The trees bowed down to the floor of Paradise throughout the woodland [?]; they bent their strong tops [?] in reverence for their Creator.
'Have you heard clearly, O creatures, the deed that Adam has done, without pure [?], against my command, against my teaching?'
Each of them went off separately to hide in the shade of the tree, and the voice of God from heaven said: 'It has not gone well with you, Adam!'
Adam, in full course, spoke his very wretched plea to God: 'If I have transgressed, my wife compelled me; she was the one who led me astray.'
God said to Adam plainly: 'Because you did not confess your sin, your descendants after you will forever be quarrelling over their guilt.'
If Adam had repented with abundant lamentation, his sins would have been fully forgiven him again.
The King of the keen kingdom himself firmly commanded his angels: 'Drive Adam, who has done no pure deed, out of Paradise to the earth.'
Then the angels went to expel Eve and Adam, a wretched pair, needy and exposed to hunger, feeble, distressed [?], stark naked.
Adam earnestly [?] begged them: 'Wait for me, holy angels, so that before I go out I may taste something of the fruit of the tree of life.'
'We will wait for you, alas the fate,' said the host of angels to Adam. 'We grieve before all [?] at what Lucifer has done.'
'Do you hear me, dear God, for the sake of your angels and your archangels? Will you grant me, by grace, something of the fruit of the tree of life?'
'He will not taste the fruit of the tree of life [?] for a great host [?]; rather, the two, your body and your soul, will be together under keen torment [?].'

Their desire overwhelmed them through a flood [?]; their fate plagued them for their transgression; a grievous gloom filled them; then from that time on came strife [?] to the two of them. From that time on Eve was apart [?].
The King, in a pure course, said to Eve and to Adam: 'You have gone from me, against my great law; you will have nothing of my free bounty [?].'
'Go into a frail, withering, troubled, ever-toilsome life, sorrowful, wretched, without generous rest [?]; the penalty for your transgression will be upon you.'
'Your children, your sons, your people will serve you every single day; it will not come to good [?], alas the deed [?], until sweat is wrung from you by force.'
'A multitude of diseases will be upon you, the parting of body and soul, anxiety and toil for each of you, old age and the decay of trembling hands.'
'Resist the temptation of the Devil every day and every single year, so that he does not carry you off with him to his house, to dreadful Hell.'
'If your deeds are pure, according to my commandments and my teachings, heaven, a shining form, will be given to each according to his counsel [?].'
The King of great, glorious heaven, who is not small; King of the renowned, everlasting world; [?] each of them; the King who spoke, in a very pure course. The King who spoke, in a pure course.
The King gave the earth as a covering [?] to Adam after his transgression; he would not have been ungrateful to God himself, had it not been for the decay [?] of his time.
Adam was a week here below after being driven out of Paradise, in sorrow, without fire, without house, without drink, without food, without clothing.
When they were in poverty, they fell into cold and hunger; great was the mutual reproach at every turn between Eve and Adam.
'O Eve, of fitting and fair form, wretched indeed was it to be turned by you [?]; cold is the outcome [?]: Paradise has cast us out through your misdeed, through your transgression.'
'Great is the good we have lost since we angered our high Prince: Paradise was ours by pure calling, with all its honours.'
'Pleasures and joy were heard by us; health, delight, pleasantness, fruitful lands, pure form, wondrous herbs, music.'
'Plenty, freedom, perfect and special peace, a holy bond with the animals, secure dwellings [?], many places, frequent converse with the angels.'
'Everlasting life, as was the custom [?], at God's right hand forever in the lands of Paradise, where God's creatures were in fair service, honouring us.'
'All the creatures under heaven that my true, dear God gave us were under our control, above every height, with their colour, in the order in which they had been arranged.'
'Fire would not burn us (a bright report), and water would not drown us, nor would a blade wound us [?] (great their valour), nor plague, nor [?] disease.'
'Among the creatures of dear God there was no creature that would come against our will, in heaven or on earth, to harm us, except the cruel Lucifer.'
'Even Lucifer, with [?], could not harm us as long as we were under the law (a bright course), obeying the command and the injunction.'
'Since we have offended dear God, who gave us all these things, every creature from every height is now set against us in opposition.'
'It is not God who has done wrong to us, O radiant, fair and lovely Eve; it is we who offended against the sovereignty, though he offered us his eternal goodness.'
Eve spoke, for she was in bondage, in misery after the transgression: 'O wonderful Adam of every plain, why do you not kill me for my sins?'
'It is I who went beyond the command, it is I who committed the transgression: it is right for you to kill me for it, my lord Adam!'
'But if I fall (a true saying) for my guilt and for my transgression, God will the more readily and clearly show mercy to you.'
'It is enough that we have angered the King,' said Adam, without pride. 'O woman, I will not commit kin-slaying on you, though I am hungry, though I am naked.'
'I will not lay my hand (a venomous deed) on my own blood or my own flesh. Though your fault is great, with [?], it was from my body that you were formed.'
'It is not right for us in any way to anger him again or to offend him again, lest the true Lord bring about, O woman, our extinction and our utter destruction.'
'Let us not go from him on a long journey to damnation in the depths of torments, lest dear God send us back again to Lucifer.'
'There is nothing good in our lot,' said Eve. 'O Adam, without clothing for us, without a warm house, without food, we shall die of hunger.'
'We had food, we had clothing, while we were without transgression; since the transgression, since our ruin [?], we have no clothing or good food.'
'O man, go around without failing, along a pleasant path on every side, to see whether you can find for a meal something of food that we might eat.'
Adam went all around, near and far; he found nothing of food that was clean to eat except the herbs of the earth.
The herbs of the earth, green their colour, are the food of the irrational animals; they were not pleasant to us for a meal after the delightful foods of Paradise.
'O Eve, let us earnestly do lasting penance and repentance, so that we may cleanse before the King of the laws something of our sins and of our transgression.'
'Instruct me about this, my lord Adam, since I do not know in any respect how penance is done.'
'Instruct me thoroughly according to your understanding and your clear sense, so that I may not myself make [?] any mistake, and so that I may not fall short in any way.'
'Let us worship the Lord together in silence, without speaking. You go into the strong river Tigris, and I will go into the river Jordan.'
'Thirty-three days, [?], you are to stay in the river Tigris; I will stay in the Jordan under discipline for forty-seven fair days.'
'Take with you a firm stone slab under your seat, under your fair feet, and I will take with me another slab like it, of similar form.'
'Set the stone in the stream and bathe while standing on it; be [?] as you are [?], until the water comes up to your neck.'
'Let your hair spread out in every direction, unfailingly, on the stream on every side. Be silent toward the [?] heaven; turn your keen eye toward the heavens.'
'Raise your two hands each time to the King of heaven of the nine orders. Pray rightly, though you are silent, for forgiveness of your sin.'
'We are not pure enough to speak to God after our transgression and our impurity, for our lips are not bright, skilled and clear; our lips are wicked and defiled.'
'Let us call on all the creatures that God shaped through his pure mystery to pray with us to the King of the laws for forgiveness of our transgression.'
'Do it this way, in good manner, and plead with the true Prince. As I have clearly appointed [?], do not move, do not stir.'
Forty-seven days, without a break, Adam spent in the river Jordan; thirty-three days dear Eve spent in the waters of the river Tigris.
Every day angels of God came from heaven, from God, to visit Adam and teach him as was fitting, until the end of nineteen days.
Then Adam made a strong plea to the river Jordan that it should fast with him to dear God, with all its many creatures.
The stream stood still in its silence [?], ceasing from its course and its [?]; the royal stream stopped its great flow until forgiveness was given to Adam.
Then the stream gathered every living creature within its bounds, the full number of its host, of every form it held, so that they were all around Adam.
They all prayed together, Adam, the stream and its many creatures; sorrowfully they raised a splendid [?] cry to the perfect host of the nine holy orders.
They asked that all the orders of the Lord should pray with them, without concealment, until God gave Adam pure forgiveness without any cancellation.
The nine orders, with their whole company, prayed to God, who received them, for forgiveness for Adam here, for his peril and his sin.
For the sake of his orders, God granted full forgiveness of Adam's sin, along with the dwelling of the earth, each [?], and the all-pure, holy, noble heaven.
Afterwards he also forgave Adam's offspring and his descendants, except anyone who does not do right and who goes against God's will in wickedness.
When the black Demon heard that forgiveness had been given to Adam, he said: 'I will go back to Eve again, clearly in a fine guise [?].'
'I will bring her out of the stream by cunning and set her on a course to death, so that my effort to disturb her devotion will not be in vain.'
Swift, eager Lucifer went, the fierce, truly cunning wolf, like a swan in the form of a bright angel, to Eve at the river Tigris.
The angel who deceived her [?] spoke to her as if pitying her: 'O generous Eve of bright form, you have been a long time in the river Tigris.'
'O woman, though your form was bright, you have changed your appearance in the rough stream. Without any strength [?] you have stayed [?]; you have killed yourself, you have destroyed yourself.'
'O woman, come up out of it to God; do not stay any longer in the harsh stream. The mighty King sent me on this errand; I have come from him out of pity for you.'
Then Eve came out of the stream and was on land drying herself. After that a cloud came over her, and she nearly died, left without breath.
Eve did not clearly recognize Lucifer of the many shapes. The good woman was grieved; her mind was in doubt.
'O Eve, what is wrong with you? You are pondering a great deal. I came to you clearly from heaven at the command of the truly dear God.'
'Let us go to Adam, O woman; do not be in [?]. We have all prayed to dear God for forgiveness of your sins.'
After that they went boldly as far as the river Jordan, to Adam, above the streams [?]: splendid Eve and Lucifer.
When Adam saw, from the river, Eve and Lucifer, trembling seized him, [?], and horror of the Devil's face filled him.
'Alas, O Eve, [?]; your coming has led you astray [?]. The man who came with you a second time [?], it is he who deceived you in Paradise.'
'O wretched Eve, without good understanding, what brought you out of the river Tigris, without the command of the King of law, without a pure angel as companion?'
When Eve heard this, the reproaches [?] that Adam made, she fell to the ground, she went into distress; she very nearly died.
'O Lucifer, O Demon, why are you pursuing us? You have overcome [?] us, it has been heard far and wide; you have brought us to ruin [?] in Paradise.'
'Since our bonds [?] have parted, do not follow us, O Lucifer: through your contention we are in bondage; we do not seek your company.'
'It was not we who took away your goodness, or who put you out of your true kingdom; it was not we who drove you [?] to be cast from the strongholds of heaven.'

'God has been good to us, O steadful, fair Eve! There was great folly here, through a folly that did not kill us [?].'

When at last God took pity on Adam, who was eating the grass, he decided and declared clearly that it was time to help Adam.

He gave them to Adam, after spreading them out, for sowing [?] each seed in its own place, and he taught him clearly how husbandry is ordered.

And afterwards he handed over to him every living animal that was on the earth: 'Let them serve you well, both the lesser and the better kinds [?].'
Seven years after that, clearly, Eve bore another child to Adam, [?] as a pledge [?]: a son whose name was Abel.
Chosen of God, bright [?], a righteous and truly perfect man, he was, by the ordinance [?] of dear God, serving his parents.
'A vision has been shown to me,' said Eve to Adam: 'the blood of Abel, with a swift [?] draught, all going into Cain.'
'Take this to heart, my lord, O Adam: there is fear in my heart and in my mind that Cain will kill Abel.'
'Woman, that will be dealt with, if it pleases God of sure mind [?]. They will not be together from now on; each of them will be in his own house.'
Adam built two houses, a house for each of them separately: a house for Cain, fair the plan, and another house for Abel.
God sent pure Gabriel to tell tidings to Adam: 'Dark Cain, rough and senseless, is plotting the killing of Abel.
'But Eve must not learn from you the tidings, which you will find most grievous: Cain will drink a draught of his blood, for he is the Devil's own son.
'So do not let it disturb your mind if Cain kills Abel; you will have a son of pure form, whose name will be Seth, the especially dear.'
Births to Adam were heard of, without peril, after the transgression: seventy sons by the eager [?] pair, and an exactly equal number of daughters.
The King raised up two sons of Adam above the very great peoples: Abel and fair Cain, with their mighty offspring.
The King gave the world with its good treasures to mankind. From long ago he was pleased with Abel, and displeased with Cain.
The King who is exalted above every form [?] — with him Cain did not make peace [?]: wicked Cain, fierce his intent, after that killed Abel.
Two hundred years, pleasant honour, was Abel's full span — no lie, it is told from of old — until he was killed by Cain.
After that the King told every one of Adam's offspring to do his will and not to kill Cain.
Whoever under heaven kills Cain for that crime, no valour will be counted to him for his deed; sevenfold vengeance will be brought upon him.
After that the great King put a clear mark of the sin on Cain, so that the crime would not be hidden: he put a lump on his forehead.
After that Cain died, without [?], at evening in the valley of Jehoshaphat, when a crooked tree struck him hard and firmly against the lump that was on his forehead.
When Cain fell there in the narrow valley of Jehoshaphat, his guilt was [?], without fruit, without profit.
Afterwards the King gave noble Seth to Adam in Abel's place, so that from him the noble families of Adam's seed descended.
It is told, and it is no idle tale, that for forty years, without harsh strife, in quiet, without sickness, without battle, until Seth began to beget offspring.
The Lord, bright with mysteries, who existed before the first elements, called forth a body from fair clay: the King who gave the earth. The King who gave the earth its beauty.
Adam's life was not short. It was without danger, as is known. He was certainly in good fortune for thirty-two [?] years beyond nine hundred.
After that a sickness came upon Adam, as distress comes. His wife Eve stayed by him faithfully in every way through his pangs.
Adam knew his fate. He said to fair, modest Eve: 'I am parting from you and from your children. I am dying of this sickness.'
'Woe, O God, a clear cry,' said Eve to Adam, 'that you will not be with me here, and that it is not I who go first!'
'Alas, it is a sad change from what was fair,' said Eve, 'O Adam! I am wretched and without strength here, while you go on ahead.'
'O Eve of bright, pure form, take this clearly into your mind: it is plain that you will not remain long here in pain after me.
'Short is the time [?] that has passed since our creation. You will not be in distress [?], it is clear, except for nine months after me.'
'Tell me truly, husband: what shall be done with your dear body? For you are sure that you will die of this, my lord, O Adam!'
'Let no foot or hand touch me, nor any person of my [?], until an angel comes from God out of heaven to arrange my dear body.
'Leave my body, in a seemly manner, in its place undisturbed. I am sure that my King will take care of the noble creature that He made of me.
'Rise, O gentle Eve, and go into your cross-vigil. Woman, send my soul from you in brightness to the right hand of God in holy heaven.
'The soul that God made for me is the one He has called back in purity. Let it go to Him whole from its dwelling, in the company of the host of bright angels [?].
'Woman, may my good King grant me truly at our meeting [?] that the anger He showed, a bright course, become a bond of affection and mercy [?].
'Beseech the noble King, Eve, so that He may come to meet me as I deserve. If He does not come to me quickly in my neglect [?], let Michael the archangel come.'
Eve rises and turns to the ground, weeping and lamenting greatly. For the space of an hour [?] she pleads with pity and with sighing.

'So great is my guilt, so great my sinfulness, that unless I have a path of lasting penance, and unless You give me forgiveness, I could not speak fully pure speech.'
Wretched Eve bends her knees to the ground to speak with the King: 'To You, O King of heaven, I offer my tears, so that the soldier Michael may come to me.
'Let the archangel come with power to cleanse the soul of Adam as it is separated from its vices, for its journey after he goes to death.'
'Rise from the ground, O Eve. Your speech has been heard very clearly. Your story has reached the kingdom of heaven, and the soldier Michael has come to you.
'The soul has gone from Adam's body, O Eve of fair form! It has gone without horror (fair the treasure) [?] to [?], O fair face!'
Eve came quickly to Adam after that, and found Adam (great the love) without any trace of breath.
Because she did not hear Adam's voice speaking to her in its fair way, her reason was overcome beyond measure, into long weeping and sorrow.
'O Eve, lift your eye and accept [?] instruction from us; set your keen, clear gaze straight up to the heavens.'
'O woman, lift your clear face to see the soul of Adam, as it is carried brightly between the hands of archangels.'
Then Eve turned to see the soul of Adam, and she saw Adam's fair, gentle soul in the company of Michael.

The choir of the host [?] of holy angels around Michael was heard; they arranged themselves in a pleasant row all around Adam's altar.

The strong smoke spread straight up through the air, so that it opened the doors of the firmament, bright beyond measure.
God came in holiness from heaven to receive Adam's soul, the royal king above all, and he sat on his royal throne.
In front of the king, on a swift, glorious course, went one splendid angel of the angels with a trumpet [?], slender, clear and bright; its sound was heard throughout the seven heavens.
At the sound of the horn, with splendid [?], the host of the nine holy orders came; their pure company was truly [?] before the royal throne of the Creator.
In choirs and choral songs they sing, fairer than jewels: 'Blessed at every time is the high king of all the elements.'
The whole perfect host of the holy, modest angels bowed down to the ground; they prayed to dear God to forgive Adam's sin.
'He is your creation, O Lord; it was you who [?] him from the [?]: they [?] upon you, bright [?]; great is your splendour, great is your mercy.'
After that the red king quickly spoke to the seraph, [?] beside the hosts with the wings of red gold,
telling him to take Adam's soul without sorrow and bathe it in the stream of the ever-flowing rivers [?], in the Acherusian lake.
So he brought Adam's bright, pure soul out of that stream, and then [?] set it before the face of the Creator.
Adam's soul itself threw itself to the ground with fair love and lay before the red king for the space of three chief hours.
After that the king put his hand on the head of Adam's soul, without [?] (fair the tale), and handed it over to Michael.
'Let it not be without music [?], bright [?], O Michael, at its great cry; take Adam's soul from here and set it in Paradise.'
'Take the bright, pure soul of noble Adam with your hosts: settle it [?], free from harm, in the third royal portion of Paradise.'

'Oil of mercy for you here in the herb ornamentum; let it be put about the body of Adam to cleanse it of its vices.'

A King without stain, without blemish [?], without attack; the world is not neglected by him [?]; not narrow [?], fair his [?]; the noble King who preserved them. The noble King who brightly preserved them.
