After that the King said to Noah and his fair children: 'The fruits of the world on every side, procure them, consume them, gather them.'
'A heavy flood that overwhelms a mighty host shall not be [?] against you (a complete pledge), as long as you see the bow of the many-coloured heaven above every plain.'
The great King, not concealing, without torment, steered the huge vessel from ocean to ocean, over [?] house, to the mountain on which it came to rest. The ark came to rest; it was heavy.
The King who bestowed the pleasant world, from the rising to the setting, with treasures, with offspring, beyond every due, on the three sons of the son of Lamech.
The King who shaped the face of the brown world, who allotted the happy order of the noble company [?]; he took without end, in right fashion [?], its boundary in length and in breadth.
He traversed [?] the boundary of the earth of every shape, a renowned, fiery power, a speckled bark [?]: from the ocean of Taprobane in the east westward to the Pillars of Hercules.
Its breadth, from north to south, whose unfailing excellence is known: from the Rhipaean [mountains], a royal dwelling [?], round to the wilderness of the Ethiopians.
The great King, who is not niggardly to his children, divided it into three mighty portions; he named them in clear, wise order: Asia, Europe and Africa.
The King gave Europe of the lands to the wondrous progeny of Japheth, with the north of Asia, triumphantly [?], as far as the courses of the river Euphrates.
The King bestowed on the progeny of Ham noble, entire Africa, as far as the Red Sea (a right onset), between Asia and Egypt.
The noble progeny of Shem, to whom God gave the chief, excellent portion of Asia, from the river Euphrates (no small thing that) to the eastern borders of the world.
Fifteen sons, a most certain tale, belonged to Japheth; twenty-seven to sound Shem; and five to gentle, modest Ham.

Though the kings of the green-hilled earth are of renowned, swift power, better than every king is the strong one of the starry courses [?], the King who bestowed the pleasant world. The King who bestowed the pleasant world.
The hosts of the seed of Adam, a vast throng, with the arts [?] of the brown southern world, were subjected, from the dwellings of assemblies [?], to the service of the Devil exceedingly.
From the region where the sun rises to its setting (a righteous wrath) they were condemned, under keen vengeance, for worshipping idols fiercely.
From the time that noble Noah died until the famous time of Abraham, not a single man among them was found apart who would entreat the Lord.
They rejected their dear God, they abandoned the true faith; east and west, south and north, suffering seized them with clear triumph.

For [?] the battle-helmet without dark colour, it is a doom-blade [?] crushing enemies; there is none unfit [?] for him among the companies of noble peoples, for [?] a sage [?] with the names of the ranked hosts [?]. The host of the seed of Adam, a vast throng.
There was born a good, victorious man of the race of every [?] — Nimrod; every hereditary company sings the tale; he was mighty over many peoples.
That Nimrod, son of Cush, son of Ham, raised his struggle with great horror: the work of a tower from the earth, without failing, so that by it he might reach the kingdom [of heaven].
He was a soldier of thousands of valorous deeds; he was learned, he was a philosopher, an excellent sage in every art; he was very learned in many grades.
By Him that was first devised [?] at the beginning for the children of Adam: His measure, clearly and purely, [?] eternal [?] on the earth.
He enumerated the world, with victory, east, west, south, north: lands, peoples, ranks of hills, miles, stadia, broad waters [?].
The historians of the noble seed of Adam were gathered by Him into one assembly; tidings of old were heard from them, how, as is clear, they were cast out of Paradise.
How dark Cain committed the first kin-slaying upon Abel; how it was avenged, a clear tale, upon the seed of Seth and upon the children of Cain.
Except Noah, one of eight in sorrow, in his capacious, ocean-great vessel, the children of Cain and the seed of old Seth were all destroyed by the Flood.
Let us serve the King of the heaven of clouds, Prince of every truly righteous kindred, so that He may not bring upon us, through His rule, a sound [?] of bitter, withering vengeance like that.
'Take my pure counsel,' said Nimrod to the children of Adam: 'build up toward heaven [?] a keen [?], and it will save you from the Flood.'
A good birth, greatness of every honour, battle-winning [?], of fiery [?] voice; the bright sun that warms every [?]; happy the people of whom he was born. A good man was born, with victory.
After that the chiefs of the proud seed of Adam took counsel: 'It would be better for us, a clear desire, to go in our bodies to heaven.'
'Let us raise a very great tower from the ground; let us make a raising equal to God; let each of us work on it in turn; let us carry it up to the holy heavenly house.'
'For if we reach the strong heavenly house, in the company of the holy angels, the Flood will not come upon us, strong rock; it is certain that we shall not die.'
Nimrod commanded everyone, with bright-cheeked heroes and fair speech, to build it, with close [?] valour, on the expanse [?] of the plain of Shinar.
Shinar son of Shem, [?] lands of streams, grandson of Noah son of Lamech, the twenty-seventh son of sound Shem: from him the plain of Shinar was named.
The hosts gathered to build Nimrod's famous tower; it was raised up — they were strong in the assembly — until it reached up above the clouds.
The King who did not allow them this confounded them through many languages, so that no one could clearly understand what one said to another.
The King who had given them one language before the building of Nimrod's tower divided it for them through His word [?], so that they were seventy-two.
The King who caused the scattering of the host, He confounded Nimrod's tower; the clarity of their skill departed [?] from the fair concord of their common language.
The King who distinguished the children of Adam by sense, by form, by ranks — no crooked reckoning, fair the rule — into seventy-two noble races.
After the counsels of noble Nimrod with the strong men of the noble assembly, without [?] it strongly destroyed [?] them, the scheme they had devised. They took counsel after that.
The King who loved Abel of the lands, Seth, Noah, Melchizedek, Enoch and Lot, a full festival, and the wondrous Abraham.
The King who chose glorious Abraham for his righteousness alone, beyond the host of the valorous seed of Adam who were worshipping idols.
He promised Abraham every victory for his coming from the great north and for going with Him southward: that he would have a land as his own forever.
The King who granted him the land of Ham [?] and the plain-lands of Canaan, so that it would be an inheritance for him afterwards, for his children and for his races.
The King with whom he went south, so that He protected him forever; with him went Lot, with troops of followers [?], southward, his brother's son.
The King who came to the glen of Mamre, to the house of wondrous Abraham, in the form of three — fervent [?] the rule — when He partook of hospitality.
The King who told Sarah that she would safely bear a son to Abraham; their offspring increased afterwards, so that they were devout [?] [fíadgenemain: meaning uncertain].
The King who saved Lot with his children, except his wife, who was turned into a pillar of salt, when He took vengeance, a wondrous blow, on the cities of Sodom.
The King who at once granted to Abraham, son of Terah son of Nahor, that he would save him from the torture [?] of torments; the bright King who loved Abel. The King who loved Abel of the lands.
The King who then gave Abraham, for propagation and for offspring, a son named Isaac. That is famous throughout the world [?].
The King who gave Isaac (it was a triumph) the daughter of Bethuel; from them were born, a great festival, Esau and Jacob.
Esau, of many tracks [?], who travelled the paths, was beloved of Isaac; and Jacob, with purities [?], was dear to his mother.

Isaac, toward the end of his life, after the struggle of deeds of pure valour [?], had a fine flock [?] of good gold [?] [dramm datta: meaning uncertain]; he was an old man, blind and without strength.
Without delay he asked his son, Esau, for a meal, with lines of learning [?], so that he might leave [?] and give him his blessing.
Rebecca, the daughter of Bethuel, who was not negligent, was listening to him, and she clearly carried out her plan to win the blessing.
While Esau was setting out into the mountain to hunt, as was true, the woman went with perfect zeal to the flock of ewes [?] of Jacob.
She killed a tender kid in the field and boiled it carefully [?] with herbs. She carried out a swift deed with clear purity [?] and prepared a meal for Isaac.
She sewed the skin of the great kid around Jacob's hand through her contest [?], to look like Esau's hand. It was a bold deed, though it was a deception.
His mother quickly spoke to Jacob, a pure festival [?]. He rose up without weakness, along the shore [?], and gave a meal to Isaac.
When the hearty meal was brought to Isaac in his chamber, in the likeness of host-leading Esau, a perfect path [?], Jacob was afraid.
'Here is an especially skilful, wholesome meal for you, O famous son of Abraham, from noble, bright Esau of the ranks of hosts, your delightful son of many triumphs.'
'Esau was not hunting, unless it is a lie told to him through fair deceit. He came early from the mountain, that is clear, if it is he who brought this meal.'
'It is I who made the keen hunt on the first slope of the mountain. Close at hand, in a short and clear time [?], I found the makings of a meal for my father.'
'Do not try to deceive me to gain the victory, O son of Bethuel's daughter! You are not Esau, the firm one [?] of the hosts; you are the cunning Jacob.'
'Do not doubt me, venerable splendour, O father, O son of Abraham. By your bright, loving affection, I am Esau; I do not speak a lie to you.'
'Give me your hand, for the purpose of touching [?], so that I may feel it, so that I may know clearly, in this pure deed, whether it is Esau or Jacob.'
'Though I put my hand in your hand, I do not hide it: I am in your gentle meeting. I know you; it is you who reared me. What causes my doubt is strong.'
'To my son Esau, victory of the arms [?], and to the sweet daughter of Bethuel: since they are likely of one clear nature, it is fitting that they should be alike.'
'Perhaps it is Esau, perfect path [?]; perhaps it is not Jacob; perhaps my lack of wisdom is plain; perhaps it is I who am deceived.'
That is an old proverb from long ago, used by every elder and every old man: the slow one does not judge [?] one thing from another [?]; but if he is blind, he will be doubtful.
A wretched, unfriendly, blind, infirm, feeble [?], completely slow person: that father is badly off in clear wisdom after his senses have left him.
'Eat the noble, wholesome dish, O holy one [?], O son of splendid Abraham! Eat your portion in the pure customary way; may it be an excellent satisfaction to you.'
Isaac then ate the dish joyfully. He raised his hand, he rose, and he bestowed his blessing.
In pure order, as it had passed between Abraham and Isaac, he gave to Jacob the blessing that had been offered to the host [?].
Twice seven years [?], without folly or sorrow, was Jacob's age when he took the birthright; fairly he shared out everything he possessed [?].
When he had given the pleasant dish to his father, the son of Abraham, he did not know what to do, out of fear that his brother would kill him [?].
His good mother said to him: 'Go, flee from your brother to the radiant dwelling of Laban. It is a fair and fitting deed, without anything shameful.'
Jacob went triumphantly to the house of Laban son of Bethuel, [?] without betrayal, at the time of the sheep-shearing.
After that he found them outside beside the radiant enclosure: Laban's two daughters, bright of colour and without fault, washing their sheep.
There they were, excellently, before [?], very bright, without noise and without anything ugly: the two daughters of Laban [?].
The youth said to them triumphantly: 'Where here is the son of Bethuel, my mother's brother, of splendid bearing, a man whose name is Laban?'
After that they welcomed the diligent youth, and one of them went off at a splendid run to tell Laban.
Laban, with his bands of warriors, came out to meet his sister's son. He poured a shower of welcome on him and brought him with him to his house.
Laban offered Jacob full wages for his herding: every little lamb speckled with black, every grey lamb, every piebald lamb.
Jacob would lay a row of small rods of speckled colour in the watering-troughs, in front of the sheep.
The flocks of sheep in turn would look at the bright, clean rods, and the colours of the rods took hold, so that the same colours appeared on the lambs.
Afterwards Laban gave him his daughters, readily and without dispute, after the herding for a time [?], in return for herding Laban's sheep.
Their names, without reproach, wise authors tell us: comely Leah, with her bands of [?], and royal Rachel.
Each of the two beautiful sisters had a handmaid. Their names, without [?]: Bilhah and fair Zilpah.
All of them together, both sisters and handmaids, without anything ugly and by proper agreement, shared the bed of the one Jacob.
They bore three times four sons, of strong and pure vigour [?]: eight from the sisters in turn, four from the handmaids.
Each mother's share of her rightful offspring, in its order, as the King of mysteries arranged all things: it is best for us to set them out separately.
Six sons were Leah's, with her bands of [?], and two sons were Rachel's. The King of the strong world assigned [?] four sons to the handmaids.
Reuben, Simeon, Levi [?], noble Issachar, Zebulun, and Judah, after God without [?]: the six sons of tear-eyed Leah.
Naphtali and bold Dan were the two victorious sons of Bilhah. Asher and Gad, fair of form, were the two sons of beautiful Zilpah.
Splendid Joseph, renowned far and wide, and fair Benjamin, the two very beautiful sons of Rachel, took seats [?] of hostages [?].
Those were the twelve sons of Jacob, grandson of Abraham, without any hatred, with their distinctions in every tribe, with their four mothers.
Seventy years he was in the north in the household of Laban son of Bethuel, until he set out for his own land, rightly [?], with his twelve sons.
When Rachel, daughter of Laban son of Bethuel, came from the north, she committed a deceit through treachery: she took with her her father's household idols.
Fierce Laban went after them, over plain, wood and mountain, until he overtook them, without any doubt, in the heat of the day in the middle of the mountain.
When glorious Rachel, the radiant daughter of Laban, saw him, she went apart, a fitting stratagem [?], as though she were in her menstrual period.
Rachel put her father's purple, fair idols down beside her; her wailing was heard, her colour changed, like a woman in childbed [?].
Laban, of bright retinues [?], left alone [?] the seat [?] on which Rachel was; it was not their custom, vigour of the nursing [?], to handle a woman in childbed [?].
Jacob triumphantly gave a great welcome to the son of Bethuel, and with bright love he allowed him to search all his saddle-bags [?] freely.
When he did not find his idols there (the women's contest was not narrow [?]), they raised on the plain a cairn of mutual oath as a covenant.
For everyone, that cairn of the covenant is a pledge that there will be no war [?], forever, between the spirited offspring of great Laban and the descendants of Jacob.
The angel of God who commands every host was wrestling with Jacob; they fought a battle, a bright contest, without death, throughout the night.
The noble angel struck Jacob, it is no lie [?], beyond the edge of his thigh [?]; from that, wondrous is the story, he was named Israel.
A messenger went with gifts from Jacob, a fair errand, to noble Esau, a bright course, so that they might be brothers.
After that Esau promised, a fair pure deed, it is no lie, that they would be without hostility, without strife [?], in friendship, as equals.
Without evil, without kin-slaying, a bright deed, according to the commandments of their brotherhood; without deceit, without shame, without betrayal, without strife, without sorcery [?].
The sons of Jacob, many were their exploits, were brothers of Dinah; because of Shechem son of Hamor, through treachery, they killed the people of his city.
Fourteen [?] years he was here, under the law of rule, in suffering [?], until he was compelled [?], his strength failing [?], to go to the land of Egypt.
The King chose, a forceful cry [?], noble Jacob over his brother, so that from his offspring, the story concludes, came the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel.
The Son promised by God from heaven proclaimed, pure, shining [?], fair and dear [?]: he is a flame above the hill of the glorious abbots, the King who gave to Abraham. That King gave to Abraham.
Jacob clearly prophesied to his offspring, all of them: 'You will all be, know it keenly, in need of the benefits of Joseph.'
Jacob sent Joseph, a branch with power [?], on a journey to Shechem, a fair step out from the house, with food for his brothers.
When Joseph reached Shechem safely, where the whole flock was, he found a man there, a bright [?], travelling his road.
The keen man asked him: 'Where have you come from, where are you going? What are you seeking, mighty cry [?], whom are you looking for?'
'I have come alone from my house with food for the herdsmen; weary, exhausted at every turn, I am seeking the sons of Jacob.'
'The sons of Jacob, of pure glory, if it is they you are seeking, have set out along the roads; they are near Dothan.'
After that Joseph came to Dothan, to his brothers, with a she-ass in his hand. She went at a swift pace and carried a load of food.
The sons of Jacob, grandson of Abraham, gathered in a group ahead of him, and each of them said to the other: 'Is this the dreamer?'
'Brothers, pay attention to my words and do nothing that is wrong. Even if some good fortune were to come to me, it is no [?] that would cast you down [?].'
'Alas, your sense is not good, Joseph, son of Rachel. You have been foolish and lack clear wisdom; your dream has surely deceived you.'
'What my God has ordained for me among the people of the earth, none of you can increase or lessen through strife.'
From then on, Joseph son of Jacob was shown a great vision of things far off. Out of envy, his brothers hated him because of the rule [that was foretold for him].
Joseph went with them to the mountain with provisions [?], in glory and pure honour. His brothers plotted to betray him, out of their own presence [?], so that they might kill him.
They would have put him to death by force had the Son of the great King not saved him. It was not the high esteem that people spoke of that protected him, nor friendship, nor kinship.
At that very time, by command of the King of holy heaven, a great company of merchants travelled to Egypt with clamour and with a train of animals.
When they met them on the plain, they sold Joseph, the youngest, their brother. He went under a good omen (a true account) and so came to be in the land of Egypt.
Iasse son of Sechis, of a noble line, was the leader of the merchants. He was from their own kinsmen (an excellent journey), and he was the one who bought Joseph.
Potiphar (my account is true) was the chief man of Egypt. He paid thirty half-ounces of silver for Joseph while he was in captivity.
When Joseph ran into the land of Egypt to his certain ruin [?], with bright wisdom and a true bearing [?], he was a full seventeen years old.
Joseph was in the land of Egypt for twice seven years (a sure triumph), until afterwards Jacob came from the north with his sons.
From then on they were in bondage under the noble rule of Joseph. For Jacob it was a true deed: what he had foretold came true. Jacob had foretold clearly
that there would be a king with holiness above every tribe. He prophesied in front of his brothers, without falsehood and without [?] (a true deed), that he would be in servitude in Egypt.
After that he came (it was a sure triumph) to the chief man in the land of Egypt. Every lasting good thing the chief had here, he placed in Joseph's power.
Then the wife of the lord who had bought him fell in love with him. Through secret, deceitful enticement she urged him to share her bed.
The youth answered her clearly: 'I do not desire dealings with women, and I am in bondage without a guide, alone in foreign lands.'
The smooth woman said to him: 'Do not refuse me [?]. What I am offering you, there are many who would welcome it.'
'Woman, a blessing on your pure face! Do not try to move me with your foolish words. As long as I live (a bright victory), I will not betray my lord.'
Because the youth had not done her will, the woman thought hard about how she could bring danger on the pure, sinless youth.
This is what the foolish woman devised while the warrior was not at home: the youth would come with her at some time into the house, to the treasures underground [?].
'Come with me, young man, to see my treasures; it is no lie. Open the lock of the house in front of me, fair Joseph the Canaanite!'
'Man, go into the house ahead of me so that I am not fearful [?] and [?], for I do not go, on a safe path, into a dark house all alone.'
After that Joseph went into the house; he was not ungentle [?] in contention [?]. He did not know of the woman's plan to betray him until he was behind the door.
When she, fair above every form, failed after clear [efforts] [?] to win union with Joseph (it was a deed of jealousy), she pressed herself upon him by force.
He went out away from her, out of her hands, naked; the woman cried out with all her might; he had parted from her in true, firm modesty.
A grievous, harsh [?] servitude came upon Joseph, the noble son of Jacob: he was put in prison, a hard deed, under the rule of false witness.

The everlasting High King of the dewy world, who could win victory in every chief contest, though fetters [?] bound his body [?] ... [?], a king with holiness above every household [?]. A king with holiness above every household.
A vision appeared, a true [?] ..., to Pharaoh, king of Egypt; there was not found for him among the sages of the plains, among his druids, anyone who could interpret it.
There was not found for the righteous one [?] over the plain of Egypt with its territories any wise man or druid or skilled sage who could interpret it clearly and plainly.
Pharaoh was in contention with his people [?] until he seized very red blades [?], with the dark druids of every household, with his sages, with his wise men.
There were with the king of Egypt, in good disposition and love [?], two foster-brothers, beyond all others at the gatherings of every household, in his ranks and in his counsels.
At his choice will, in his house [?], in his covenants and his pure agreements [?]: one of the men was from Egypt, of fair repute [?]; the other, brightly righteous, from Africa.

They were, without sorrow, very renowned [?] in their friendship and their fosterage; they were kin through their mothers (literally: mother's brother), a clear relationship, each of them to the other.
The king of Africa asked of them, a perfect [?] utterance, that there should be a payment of red gold, as much as they might take from every share, provided only that they killed Pharaoh.
After that they attempted an attack upon him, upon Pharaoh, upon the high prince; one of the men failed in his valour [?], for his father was from Egypt.
The other man, from noble Africa, with a battle-rod of a full cauldron [?], threw his body into the fight; he attempted to kill Pharaoh.
They were seized by the king; they were ... [?] in dishonour; they were put in fetters for a long time in the prison with Joseph.
Dreams appeared to them that very night at once, in the bondage of the tormenting prison ... [?]; their state of mind was sorrowful.
Joseph, with bright glory, gave them a just judgment on their dreams: as it was certain and profitable forever, so it was fulfilled.
'Tomorrow one of the men, who was not beloved, will be hanged; the other will be, in full peace, in favour with the high king.'
The king, by the learning of appearances [?], concerning the matters of his dream, was in gloom [?] ... [?]—it was not pleasant—angry with his good men.
The young man told him, a bright deed: 'Do not be troubled about your dream: there is in the prison, without doubt, a man who will solve your riddles [?].'
'A man who gave judgment on a vision, on a course [?], to the two of us when we were in captivity; as his fair understanding foretold, so it came to pass.'
After that noble Joseph was brought by a fair summons out of the prison, before the host of Egypt, a wondrous deed, so that he was in the presence of Pharaoh.
Pharaoh himself asked him before the host, very clearly: 'Do not be sad; tell the tidings: what people are you of, or what kindred?'
Joseph told with grace, steadily, with ... [?]: 'It is not right to tell a lie before a dread king; I am from the north, from the land of Canaan.'
'It is not that which brings me the summons [?]: my father was a grandson of Abraham, that Abraham whom we speak of from long ago [?], who was of no weak stock of the Chaldeans.'
'It has been foretold from long ago, behold, O Pharaoh of pure sense! The famous [?], fair world will be full of it, of the God whom Abraham fervently worships.'
'A vision appeared to me, a wondrous sound; its [?] ember burned me. Among the wise minds of Egypt I have found no one who could interpret it rightly.'
'Tell the splendid dream,' said fair, modest [?] Joseph. 'Let us hear from you, without [?] and without [?], the vision and how it appeared to you.'
'What appeared to me, O gracious son: every lasting good will be given to you if you give a true judgment on it. There will be no lack of honour for you.'
'It will be a true judgment that I give, O prince,' said ever-gracious Joseph, 'a clear deed of great renown in every way, without falsehood and without confusion.'
'Seven fat cows appeared to me, and seven lean cows, a wondrous thing. The seven lean cows, a clear marvel, devoured the seven fat cows.'
'Seven ears full of grain, and seven thin ears, a strange meeting. The seven thin ones, it was sad indeed, devoured the seven ears full of grain.'
'I heard the voice speaking [?] to me: "Listen, O Pharaoh not [?]: the mystery is great, a bright onrush [?]; there is a torrent [?] in your dream."'
'"Give to my mind without betrayal [?], O distinguished one [?] of every understanding [?]: the world will be full, under clouds of renown, of the tales of this vision."'
'"If anyone gives a true judgment on it, on this wondrous dream, he will obtain [?] the wealth of the world, and he will redeem [?] himself from lasting bondage."'
'The man who gives a clear and proper judgment on the dream will have, without poverty or weakness [?], of great powers [?], a share with him [?] in the kingship.'
So that the bright, full [?] dream may be revealed to you without doubt, a fair deed, O servant without ugliness [?], pray to the wondrous God of Abraham.
'You will have from me the esteem of the host, you will have rank, you will have honour, if you truly manage in every way to interpret the vision.'
'Let pledges [?] be given to me without grief,' said Joseph with noble love, 'as the spoken word promised, so that it may be fulfilled completely.'
'You will have from me the pledge of God himself, you will have my dignity fully and completely: sun and moon together, sea and land, dew and [?].'
Joseph clearly told Pharaoh his dream, with close, swift [?] and with regular [?].
Jacob's young son, full of grace, was the bright, precious gem [?]. Because he was upright in his right dealing, he took the high-kingship of Egypt.
The precious dream, of right measure [?], was terrifying to the host of Egypt: like a storm of thunder [?] was the vision that appeared to Pharaoh. A vision appeared, a right [?].
The King, who through grace chose [?] from long ago, through smooth, very clear providence [?], so that Joseph, with his host [?], was over noble, great Egypt.
There were seven full years together, prosperous, sound and happy, from when Joseph took his glory of valour [?] until the time of the great famine.
Joseph ordered, a sensible deed, that until the end of seven years they should take, though his authority was great, neither clothing nor gold nor silver.
Joseph would take no due from the peoples except food, with fair dealings, a right race [?], as owed to the king of Egypt.
He gathered what he found during the seven years into strong, secure fortresses, into [?] storehouses [?].
A harsh, fierce famine came upon them; it struck them [?] grievously [?]. It withered them out of shape [?] and filled them with sorrow and despair.
All the peoples of Egypt gave Joseph, in return for food, all the gold and silver they held under their power, however great it was.
They gave themselves to the king in bondage in return for their food, so that they would not meet death by famine, stark naked [?].
Joseph fed, more than any other clan, the hosts of the men of Egypt around Pharaoh. It was the service of rule, a noble undertaking, for five full years.
Before every host, along with fair-red Pharaoh, he fed without stint sixteen hundred thousand (a dear measure) and twenty hundred thousands.
Besides the lawful dues of the men of art and the chief poets, swift druids from every plain, harpers, bands of poets, and jugglers.
Besides slaves (a proper measure), an easy host for attendance, fair women in blooming companies, and splendid sons and daughters.
Besides the host that woe had filled, the wretched peoples from every quarter, who came after [?] under discipline [?] to buy in the land of Egypt.
The King blessed him over every plain, without blemish, without evil, without failing, so that noble Joseph son of Jacob was the ruler of every great plain.

King of heaven, of royal fame, who sets the bounds of every complete company, a shield [?] for battle from every plain [?], the King through whose grace he chose [?]. The King through whose grace he chose [?] from afar.
In the second year (a pleasing account), after the bitter, fierce famine had taken hold, the children of Jacob went (it was a right deed) to buy food in the land of Egypt.
They travelled across rough wild places, through the wonderful lands of Egypt, on the track of the host, wretched [?], to the people among whom the high king was.
Weariness filled them and sadness seized them on their journeys from their own land: no knowledge of the way, no guide, no language in unknown lands.
After their journeys they were anxious about their swift deeds and their foolish ways [?], before hosts from every plain: wretched, sorrowful and tearful.
Their spirit was weary; [?] urged them [?]. With no one to bring them, the question weighed on them, until they came to the high king of their answer [?].
They went through the midst of the host, sorrowful, [?] equally wretched, and they halted (a good truth) in the presence of the high king.
He sent swift messengers from him to meet them, cleverly and quickly, when he recognised the right deed, the renowned [?] king of Egypt.

Afterwards they went to their land, just as he had sent them off, without deceit; they brought [?] a gift from God to Jacob [?].
Afterwards they reached their house free, safe and in good spirits: good fortune came to them, [?] plentiful abundance [?], in the second year. In the second year, a pleasing account.
Noble Jacob gave thanks to his Lord, a complete deed, because his children, pure and upright men, had found a welcome with the king of Egypt.
Because He had guided them on a peaceful course [?] through the vast lands of the Nile, He had kept them from harm on every plain [?] and set them on an excellent path.
Because He brought them back, no feeble thing, from every walled city [?] with great [?], so that they came gratefully to their house, he gave thanks to his high king. Noble Jacob gave thanks.
Jacob's wonderful sons took a sound counsel: to go the same way once again into the land of Egypt.
They went on safe paths, their whole company without mishap, a strong band [?] across every land, until they reached the high king.
They found plenty and, without anger, a great welcome from the king; as was pleasing to right reason, they had their trading at once.
Joseph took a new cup and put it into the hand of a man of his household: "On my instruction [?], put it into the sacks of the Canaanites to betray them."
They went to their land without offence [?]; they had not displeased the king. Since every journey had been granted to them with success, Joseph's blessing was upon them.
When the company were on the plain, about a mile from the city, a fierce, swift band set out after them to seize them, no mistake about their fate [?].
They were not on their guard against pursuit; they were surrounded [?] at once and brought harshly from the plain back to the city [?].

The king addressed them and said to them at once: "Sad is your lot, you bright company: you have all been caught as thieves."
"Since you, no pleasant matter, are the thieves beyond dispute, I declare that the guilty one [?] among you is to be hanged, that one man alone."

"Go on your way [?] and leave Benjamin, since it is with him, a clear point of the inquiry [?], that the cup of Egypt was found."
"The youngest of the family, a bright deed, [?] true men [?]: he is the dearest of our company to our father, to Jacob."
"We ask something of you, if it does not displease you, O king of Egypt: though you keep us [?] at your will, set Benjamin free."

'O sons of noble Jacob, harsh offspring of Abraham, without help of renown, without any fame, you have fallen into guilt.'
They put forward a tale without force, and they bowed down before the high king: 'We call God to witness, [?], that you may save us from this guilt.'
'Make [?] without weakness, [?] strong, firm [?]; reveal against anyone great malice: you have done a dangerous deed.'

'We tried to drown him, it was a wretched deed; we tormented Jacob; we betrayed a dear one of our kin; we sold our one brother.'

'It was not right for you to drown me; long have you been in hiding [?]; the help of God has come to us, O wondrous race of Jacob!'
'There will be a bond [?] of victory at our meeting, O descendants of noble Abraham! Without a deed of guilt [?], through dear [?], it is I whom you sold.'
They marvelled at him [?], they gave thanks for the meeting, they turned their lament fittingly, they wept for great joy.
'Set out boldly, it is not wretched for you; go to fetch Jacob without sorrow; broad is the right, strong the power in Egypt.'
Afterwards the King brought Jacob from the north with his sons, when they went southward on the journey, in the name of Joseph, into Egypt.
Then they came southward to Joseph, into his neighbourhood; the best of every dwelling Joseph gave to his brothers.
Jacob was, a right deed, without trouble in the lands of Egypt, together with his offspring and their fame, for seventy-two years.
Great was the love with which He brought Abraham from afar out of Chaldea; it is He who granted them, according to right justice, what they did. They made a just counsel.
Then noble Joseph died; they had no freedom of noble rank: the men of Egypt, so great their wickedness, put them under heavy slavery.
They enslaved them to their will after the death of wondrous Joseph; such slavery, a clear burden, [?] forever [?].
Many of the offspring of the host of Israel—it was a wretched tale—were born with fair eyes and a dear voice [?]; they would strike off their heads.
Many evils, not right, the host of Egypt inflicted on them: there was no slavery more fiery; they slew their firstborn.
Though the slavery that came was heavy, God was helping them: as many as the hosts would crush, they would increase every single hour.
Joseph son of noble Jacob, son of Isaac, son of Abraham, spent ten score years in Egypt according to the rules of law.
He went to death [?], sinless sport, on the path of the elders, a wise, noble, dear man; he left two sons, good their grace, Manasseh and Ephraim.

Moses was born, a clear course, in the time of the heavy slavery: though his form was fair, he was cast out into the stream of the Nile to drown him.
Termuth found him, a right deed, the daughter of Pharaoh king of Egypt, in the stream as she was washing her hands; fair and generous, steadfast, white and modest.
After that she commanded her maidservants to bring out from the strand the little boy of pure form, for God had put him into her mind.

Jesus without sorrow — pure utterance — without a mighty earthly father: every lord rejoiced at the bright deed in the time when he was born. Moses was born, of bright manner.

Pharaoh rightly proclaimed to the famous men of Egypt that there should be no protection for him anywhere: only his death or his banishment.

The King who sustains all the hosts, he is the ruler of red gold [?]; he follows no crookedness, no falsehood, no doubt. The King gave him the smooth rod. The King gave a smooth rod.

Moses did a dear deed, in the name of the King of heaven (the word of God before princes): from his rod he made a serpent.

The stewards [?] are [?] to the King of holy, noble heaven, who brought great vengeance on the land, on the king whom [?] the King addressed. The King spoke firmly to Moses.

The Egyptians let them go free, in their troops and in their great hosts. In this way they set out on their journey along the wondrous paths of Egypt.

The King who called Moses to Him for fine deeds on Mount Sinai, without drink, without food — a clear manner — to the end of forty days.

While Moses was on the mountain (it was not hidden [?]), a deed was done by them, and it was not a right deed: a calf fashioned [?] of red gold.
After that, worse than any story, the tribes of the children of Israel, both men and women, without grace, all went to worship it.
Rejecting the King of the pure angels was a great deed of the great host, along with the eating of the rough grass before the image of the lifeless calf.
The Lord was rightly angry with them, with the faithless race of Jacob. He meant to cast the host under the earth in a single hour.

In the presence of God (he was a tower of godliness), learning the rule in royal mystery on Mount Sinai (a shining path), Moses was there a long time. While Moses was on the mountain.
After that Moses forcefully ordered the host that was with him to kill the great host for the space of three hours,
so that no one should spare (a bloody cry) his mother or father, or his brother ([?]), or his kinsman, or his friend.
Moses cut down (a shining deed) both beasts and people, men, boys and women alike. He put them under the swords of vengeance.
After that he ground up the image of the red gold of the demon. He gave it to the great host to drink, and there was no pity in it.
God commanded (a shining thunder) a teaching that gave no protection to kin, according to the order of wisdom (a bloody restraint), and He gave the command to Moses. Moses forcefully commanded it.
Some time later a grievous plague came upon them, a disease of the inner parts. Many of the host died of the very fierce, very red flood [?].
The King spoke to them clearly: "Make a bronze serpent. Let it be raised with grace on a tree above the host, for healing.
"Whoever on the plain looks at the tree and the serpent will be whole, whatever they do; they will not die of the disease."
It stands there as a figure of Christ, who came to save them. He was raised on a tree with grace; it was for our sake that He was crucified.
Whoever looks there to Jesus Christ, who was [?] for our sake, will have heaven, a firm dwelling, in everlasting fellowship with the archangels.
The hosts of Adam's seed besides, saints and sinners alike, a great many of every bright rank, are gathered with Moses.

The tribe of Levi, a beloved band, at the will of the King of the saints: seventy men at a time [?] to help with it and to serve it.

The rod of Aaron, it was a wondrous treasure, of great glory, pure, before the bright Face; under blossom, a leaf of holy fragrance, bearing the fruit of every good treasure.
In the vessel full of manna, six hundred ounces of gold without [?]; in the proper chief candlestick, three hundred ounces of sure red gold.
Seven lasting branches, a triumph of [?], on the blood-red candlestick; they were made of bright pure gold, and on them were seven lamps.
Bright cups, round, without any cover [?], [?] pleasant and distinctive [?]; into them drops were poured which lit the lamps.
Seven hundred ounces in the great table, with four crosses of red gold; on it seventy-two [?] of thick unleavened bread.
The candlestick on the south side, fair, lamp-like, without disdain; the table on the north, an offering of mystery, with the thick loaves.
Many cups, curled goblets, many vessels in plenty, splendid; many dishes for lofty minds, with figures of red gold.
All of gold, many figures, with fine craftsmanship, no uncertain manner; the [?], with floods of [?], the [?] in the [?] vessels.
With rows of lamps, a light of [?], which shone round about in the tabernacle; bright, glorious candlesticks, they were shaped of red gold.
They were lit diligently at all times, oil and wax together, after being poured in for kindling, without failing, without being put out.
A house for the gathering of everyone, without dispute, without talk, without merriment, without sorrow of [?]; light both day and night.
A divine temple, a shelter of every splendour, a most fair, most beloved dwelling, for speaking with God here for a time, for instruction, for teaching.
Foolish folk did not frequent it, women or boys or bands of warriors; no one went from his place, except righteous, truly steadfast folk.
Wretched folk, godly and fitting folk, former laymen and laywomen, hosts old, pleasant, sorrowful, with floods of crying, round about it from outside.
Let virgins, priests and readers go into the church accordingly: a humble folk, with steady step, after penance, after pure confession.
The order of clergy, it was right and proper, let them bow down diligently to the altar; let them be steadfast, not fickle, being quiet and in fear.
Let each take his task in turn according to Aaron son of Amram, pure and cleansed, for his priests, at the word of the high priest.
Let there be done by you, according to the custom of every season, always in the tabernacle, the morning offering, great its renown [?], and the evening offering.
The fragrance of the herbs on every side, with the presence [?] of the Holy Spirit; renown with splendour, for frequent resort [?], for health, for lasting satisfaction [?].
The King said to them: 'Set out a row around the church on each side, on the enclosure with [?], with pure-white linen hangings.'
'The door of the enclosure to the south, a fair, bright path that is not narrow [?], for the service of God, a divine cry, for the resort of the great hosts.'
'Let there not be in your dwelling, a deadly thing, between the [?] of the chancel [?] and the sun: a path of the Holy Spirit set apart, for service, for resort.'
Thus was the church in its beauty, as the high King had laid it out; above every plain it excelled, without excess, without lack.
The King who gave them a law under rules, who brought them out of the lands of Egypt, he is prince of the hosts, sound [?], the King who spoke to them. The King spoke to them without sorrow.
The King spoke to them a new address for setting the host in order around the noble, lofty church: three tribes on each single quarter.
Three tribes, with splendour, in the east, toward the rising of the [?] sun; three on the west side in a row, toward the true setting.
Three tribes on the south side, without concealment, with excellence of true benefit [?]; three, who gathered every triumph, by the church to the true north.
The King spoke to them [?], for the offering, for the celebration: the tribe of Levi, most numerous [?], without attack [?], in the middle, around the church.
The second son of noble Joseph, Manasseh, of thousands of great rank, settled according to the law of God in the place of the tribe of Levi.
The King put Aaron in authority so that he was chief priest, and Moses, greater than any other, in the leadership of the people.

King of proud [?] life, lasting his might [?], King of the world [?] which he created, King above every king, without strife, just; the King spoke the address to them. The King spoke to them a new address.
After that the host was envious of Moses and of Aaron, concerning the law of the priest, a noble rule, and concerning the leadership.
After that, swiftly, through pride, in their course, there rose up against Moses, of noble bearing, Korah, Abiram, Dathan.
The King avenged that upon themselves and upon their hosts: fire burned them, floods of fury [?], and the earth swallowed them.
The host rose up, to whom battle was customary, when it was [?] of a brother [?]; they went, the number of the land [?], as far as the tabernacle.
The angel slew them plainly because of their anger against Moses: fourteen thousand of the host, with a hundred swift leaders who perished [?].
Against the wondrous, noble sons they attempted a brave, full battle; the host in their ranks on every side [?], fierce it was, envious. After that the host was envious.
Moses tells the host, so that they might not be in commotion, that a rod from each tribe, without restriction, should be brought by them to the church.
Whosever rod, lasting fragrance, should sprout with full fruit, let him take, by the will of God, a bright protection, the noble order of the priests.
Moses plants for them each rod; it was the resolving of a great question: the rod of Aaron, wondrous its fragrance, shone with full fruit.
Thereby Aaron was ordained to the priesthood of the people: the pride of the fierce ones was humbled, every murmuring was rebuked.

Moses, great and pure, whom princes praised, gathered the host's [?] in their noble division, with wise [?] stakes [?], a call without concealment; according to the courses of the rule he speaks. Moses speaks to the host.
Everyone heard, a renown without restriction, when Aaron went to the church, on each side of his divine mantle little bells sang music.
Its twice seventy [bells], exact and fitting, fastened to a firm band [?] of red gold, and a bright apple of gold between every two little bells.
After it had been fashioned — a glorious remembrance — the angled hood [?] of Aaron; after its adorning [?], its form was defined; after its arranging, after its setting in place.
Aaron, who was more wonderful than any other, used to sit in the tabernacle, without reproach, of godly rank, of fair speech [?], in his ridged chair of red gold.
The fitting chair, fair its form, without reproach, for the chief priest; a sufficient treasure [?] before every eager company; its back against the pure pillar [?].
Each of them used to come to his assembly from every side around the sanctuary — a synod of elders, noble hosts; they used to bring the law according to the canon [?].
His four sons — a bright work — of noble Aaron son of Amram, used to be there with generous speech [?], fair the rule, over the holy altar of the offerings.
The hosts of the priests, in ranks of grades, each of them with his back to the fair board [?], of the holy church that was beautiful, at the adornment of the fair choir.
The lower grades were there according to their distinction [?]: the deacons, the subdeacons, for lighting candles — a proper task — for service, for ministering.

The host that used to be here at the feast on every side around the church, with sweet-sounding melodies, with rows of [?], with harmonious music that was heard. Everyone heard it — renown without restriction.
Moses was wearied — a complete manner [?] — by many affairs, by discussion, by his teaching in every form, by its arranging, by its setting in order.
By setting everyone under the yoke, because of the great number of the many grades; by bringing pure speech into harmony; by their instruction; by their governing.
By keeping them whole [?], under a law of mystery, by their ranking according to the order of the camps, in fear of God [?], without pride, without excess.
His kinsman by marriage clearly gave good counsel to Moses: 'Ask the radiant King — a course [?] — that someone from the host may help you.'
After that Moses — a bright deed — asked the noble King of heaven that someone from the host might be chosen to help him with every discussion.
The King, through his grace, chose from the host, prosperous for sitting [?], to decide shrewd cases, two men and ten and three score.
Six certain ones of them from each tribe, judges wise of mind, for settling cases — a bright deed — in the presence of most pure Moses.

With clear actions, with restrained words, lofty and strong at assembly, with Moses of great dignity, without failing; though he was praiseworthy, he was wearied. Moses was wearied — a complete manner [?].
On the noble sabbaths, on the truly holy feasts, the great hosts of the children of Israel used to come to the church with strong desire.
Each of them used to come from every side with offerings to his Lord; many were the hosts of his [?] toward the tabernacle.
Moses used to come there with triumph, the helmet of wisdom of every great host: he was distinguished beyond every face; a pure veil was over his bright face.
Whether to the church or to the assembly or to the true company of his council, seventy-two — a proper measure — was the number who would be in his fair company.
No youths, no foolish folk, but a choice of generous, truly wise men, to govern them — harmonious rule — for pleadings, for judgment.
To listen for a while to hymns, to purity [?], to teaching, streams of the hosts from every tribe used to come on the sabbaths. On the noble sabbaths.
Moses, good and great, without the folly of treachery, commanded Aaron, on behalf of the host, with the will of discipline, to go to perform [?] the offerings.
Aaron rose for the assembly, with full youth, in the sanctuary; it was a complete step of the dear equal rank in the assembly of the pure angels.
The angel comes from heaven to meet Aaron, the beloved, and tells him faultlessly the law of the children of Israel.
Aaron in turn relates it to Moses, leaving out nothing of much account: the pure precepts, the chants [?], the pure commandments.
Moses relates it without concealment to his peoples, to his good people, so that there should be no one of the host [?] who would go from him without instruction.

He went clearly, without delay [?], to speak with God in the sanctuary (an original word, a pledge without betrayal [?]), since it was fitting that he should be commanded. Great good was commanded to Moses.
The King fed them according to the order of a rule for a space of forty years in the wilderness (a distinguished story), the twelve tribes of the children of Israel.
The King gave them manna from heaven as profitable, sure, dear food, and flocks of birds of his own will, so that they would not be without fresh meat.
The King gave them a stream of cold water out of the bright, very hard rock; every taste under heaven that they liked they would find in that water.
The twelve tribes without dwelling, with women, children and strong men: as bright as the sun was the hue of the bright King who fed them. The King fed them according to the order of a rule.
Miriam, noble daughter of Amram, fair and white, who was like one of noble rank [?]: she did a great evil deed that [?] her fame, for she was envious of her brothers.
Leprosy seized her, her colour changed, before the eyes of the prosperous host; had it not been for Moses, a swift deed [?], she would have died of that leprosy.
A shapely person, choice of a company, a stately, dignified woman, without another [?] in appearance; a good sister to Moses was Miriam. Miriam, noble daughter of Amram.
When the host reached the famous, very red Arnon, they sent from them a band [?] from their tribes to spy out the land.
They chose out, separately, one wise man from each tribe; they sent them on a safe road on a circuit around the borders of Canaan,
so that they might view, without betrayal, the great number of its cities, how full of valour its hosts, how many its companies [?];
how prosperous its inhabitants, how abundant its many cattle, how plentiful its herbs, how fair its plains.
When they went on the road, no mishap befell them, until they reached (a clear labour) the end of forty days.
When they had viewed the land, both smooth and rough, they came back to the wilderness in a faithless manner.
Many a conflict, many a dreadful slaughter [?], many a [?] to tell of, many a rough, fierce battle was fought [?] until it reached the Arnon. When the host reached it.
They began to revile their Lord in their speeches [?] in their great assembly: 'Your God has deceived you for ever; long has he been deceiving you.'
'We found a cold, stormy land, rough, harsh, fruitless, with many troops, strong their [?], with an abundance of serpents;
'with many hard champions, and with the strength of its great host, with ugly grey weapons, with spears, with deadly weapons;
'with chosen heroes of battles, with towers of strong soldiers, with brave cities, strong, secure, impregnable.'
Satan tried to turn them to blaspheme their great Lord; the wretched ones, through whom [?] ..., accepted the command of the Devil. They began to revile their Lord.
After that the story was turned about by Joshua and Caleb: 'False is what comes to them from their [?]; do not believe your brothers!
'We found a great, wealthy land, prosperous, inhabited, fruitful, with corn and milk, [?], with wine, with honey, with fine wheat.'
'It will break before you over every people. You will be victorious, with pure triumph. All will be yours, every region [?], both land and cities.'
'With rich and secure treasures, with lofty things, with many gifts, with lands, peoples and hills of assembly, as was promised to Abraham.'
Though [?] ... was bound [?] ... a cloud [?] from every tribe ... [?]; after that the story changed. After that the story changed.
After that my dear God destroyed the fierce, enormous people, so that the firm earth swallowed them, putting them beneath the slopes of a broad valley.
Moses, without sorrow [?], says to them that were it not for Joshua and Caleb, they would all have gone to a single death, like a bird that a snare closes around.
'There is a sorrowful journey of forty days from here to the land of Canaan; the journey will be stretched out, made longer by it, to the end of forty years.'
'Not one of the twelve tribes will reach [?] the border of Canaan (a decisive tale), except Joshua and Caleb.'
'They will not reach the land of Canaan, as far as the sea's wall, because of their blasphemy; but those who remain, their sons, will make the famous journey after they have been buried.'
After that my divine God said to Moses, in very truth: 'Old men and horsemen [?] will waste away on it continually, in exile in the wildernesses.'

Were it not for Joshua, abundant in grace, and Caleb, the just and wise, my dear God would after that have destroyed them, putting them under the surface of the earth. After that my dear God destroyed them.
Their fame went out on every side, with tales of their mighty warriors, so that every people was filled with grief for fear of their great host.
Everyone from every tribe came against the noble, unfamiliar [?] host: a host from every land (sure enough), with the many thousands of Moab.
A trembling of terror seized them, both land and cities. The strength of the hosts and their onset was quenched, with no deed, no valour, no weapons.
Every warrior, well-equipped [?], fierce, bitter and harsh, mustered against the host; but no armed, strong people was found among them who could stand against the children of Israel.
They gathered against them, in a bright tumult, four equally ready battalions: Sihon, Bashan (a warlike host), famous Moab, and Ammon.
It broke before them in a swift onrush upon those four hosts, so that they were hacked to pieces in the bloody battle on the high rocks of Arnon.
There fell there in the fighting, on the blood-red mountains, sixty-six hundred on the ground, besides seven thousand. It was a great slaughter.
The King raised them up [?], with fearful blows [?], with bloody battles and contests. After that their undimmed fame went out on every side, afterwards [?]. Their fame went out on every side.
They sent from among them for bold Balaam (he was a druid, he was just, he was fit [?]), to curse them from every side through the words of his druidry.
Balaam came on his bright mare on behalf of the great host, so that they would not falter [?] in battle, to the people of God, to curse them.
The angel of God came [?] to meet foolish-tongued Balaam. He did not let him go west or east from the place where he stood.
Foolish Balaam began to beat his steed on every side, until the mare spoke to him, a famous and shaming rebuke.
'Why do you beat me under you, Balaam, with your anger and your fury? The angel of God does not let me go to either side, with his red sword of fire.'
The leader of the host commanded Balaam, who had no pure virtue: 'From the place where you are, through treachery [?], make your curse.'
Balaam opened his mouth with a beautiful and very dear utterance. In that hour it was granted fully [?]: he sang nothing but blessing.
Balaam raised his clear voice to address the great host. He blessed them, a bright deed; he was not able to [carry out] his prohibition [?] against them.
No created person has control over all of their speech. It is certain that it lies in the hand of the fair Lord, who shaped heaven and earth.

The son of Beor, a contender against lively companies, was a [?] plague against a harsh [?]. On the noble road was a separate tribulation [?], because they sent a fierce wolf. They sent bold Balaam from among them.
A king who guided them, a king who fed them, a king who freed them on their journey, in the wilderness for that long time [?]: forty years for them.
A king who gave pure counsel to Moses and his hosts, to go to a land of dwellings without any bondage [?], after the forty [years] were completed.
A king who spoke to them in every way: 'It is time for you to leave the wilderness for the noble, enduring, whole land that was promised to Abraham.'
'Rise up onto a prosperous road. Do not be fearful or afraid. I will free you from every battle, both at the end and at the beginning.'
'Though the hosts are numerous, though the very red kings are many, they will not withstand you on any plain, in battles or in contests.'
A king who gave them food [?] at first [?], to the twelve tribes; for the king from afar, pure his splendour, is the bright king who guided them. A king who guided them, a king who fed them.
'Hear my commandments clearly. Do not be hard-hearted, to conceal [them]. Do not make with them, a bold onset, any alliance, friendship or marriage.'
'Keep your hand from the idol [?] of [?] fighting, from lying, from false testimony; without covetousness, without bright desire, except fairness toward one another [?].'
'Without theft, without slander, a fair deed; without adultery, without murder; honour of parents, a pure course; love of God and of the neighbour.'
'Keep the Passover according to the order of the rule each single year, from the fifteenth day, it is a sure right, to the excellent twenty-first.'
'Perfect, steadfast, [?] without concealment, learning and teaching, with the ten commandments, a bright [?]; keep the law of circumcision.'
'With the tithes, a living certainty, the first-fruits and the firstborn, in honour to God, a zealous call [?], always in the tabernacle.'
'Everyone with their alms afterwards, according to law, according to their devotion, according to the secrets of a righteous heart, always at the pure altar.'
'Do not forget God's commandment, the purity of humble prayer. Do not blaspheme dear God; be not [?] taught [?]; hear.' 'Hear my commandments clearly.'
Arrange the whole church always in the middle of the host: six hosts before it, a royal cry, and six hosts behind it.
No one of the host of the children of Israel would dare to move, with foot or hand, [?] a board of the tabernacle.
The tribe of Levi with [?] around the church without [?], to carry it in every way, to spread it out, to set it up.
The household of the priests, under discipline, carrying the linen cloths; they were a team, in ranks of rows, around the church on the outside.
The band of the deacons, certain for everyone, carried the curtains with the coverings, in a bright manner, with the fastenings of the ridge-poles [?].
The host of the priests, a famous assembly, carried the fair boards with every fitting, fair their splendour, with their bases of white bronze.
The council of the elders apart, as they stand in their array, go forth according to God's commandments to carry the sanctuary.
The four sons of Aaron the high priest, with their strength [?], according to the order of the rule, a bright onset, carried the ark.
The noble ark above the host, after it was made of red gold, with its implements, a great deed, with a pitcher full of good treasure.
Wonderful Aaron, high his fame [?], who was a noble priest above nobles; the ten commandments of God, a most upright custom, upon their breasts forever.
The tribe of Levi with its numbers of [?]: they were not to be distracted by the affairs of the world, a shelter of renown, by business or by fighting.
Not portions of land in the north, nor service of a mighty kingship, nor care or toil, a clear course, but the law of their church.
The King who ordained them, a perfect course, between church and host: the church at his will, very clearly, the host at the will of the church.
The church with its grades, elders, hosts, noble crafts, bands [?], herds [?] over every plain, high and splendid ones, he ordains. He ordains the perfect church.
Moses often says to them, when he was weary, an elder, an old man: 'Joshua son of Nun, a clear bond [?], will be leader after me.'
Moses son of Amram, son of Kohath, son of Levi, son of Jacob, son of Isaac, son of perfect Abraham, son of dear Terah, son of Nahor,
son of fair Reu, a swift onrush, son of noble Serug, son of Eber, son of sound Shelah, with ranks of valour, son of Peleg, son of Arphaxad,
son of comely Shem, with ranks of lands, son of noble Noah, son of Lamech, son of youthful-formed Methuselah, and son of noble Enoch,
son of Jared, with [?] of lords, son of good, praiseworthy Mahalalel, son of Cainan, son of noble Enosh, son of especially dear Seth, son of Adam.
Adam son of God, with worthy meetings [?], whom the fair, modest Lord created [?]; clear in every perfect art, he is the forefather of our great host.
Moses spent, in a fine manner, in youth and in warriorhood, according to the order of rule and the courses of law, forty years in Egypt.
Another forty, smoothly [?], in kinship by marriage with the chief priest, above Mount Horeb, [?] deed, in exile from Pharaoh.
Another forty, perfect fame, in the wilderness before the host, at the command of the King of cloudy heaven, guiding the children of Israel.
That makes six score years, without excess, without lack, the life of Moses, in thousands of verses [?], as the scripture fully tells.
The King called Moses out with him, the [?] pure leader, and took him apart from the host when his time came.
When Moses was parted from his host, with many movements [?], there was none of them who knew for certain his burial or his death [?].
The son of Amram was high king of the host, with gentle [?] contention, with perpetual victory, until the end of his life, a firm [?] judgement; Moses often used to speak. Moses often speaks to them.
The number of their true men who would show wrath in bloody, red-sworded battle: seventeen hundred and thirty, a dear sound, over seven hundred thousand.
That is the number of them that remained of their tribes, without miscounting, after the death of their fathers, in every way, after their destruction in the wilderness.
All were dead in that wilderness, their fathers and their grandfathers, without one man alive under cloudy heaven except Joshua and Caleb.
The King who destroyed them through [?] in return for their pride destroyed them, through their harsh thought, for the sin of their reviling, in the one place.
It is fitting that this be a warning to everyone, likewise forever until Doomsday, to anyone at work, a clear [?]: foolish is the reviling of the elders.
Without counting servants or households, sons, women or daughters, over every plain, with deeds of wise valour, full warriors in their full number. The number of their true men who would show wrath.
The King who ordained the son of Nun, Joshua, with an abundance of many mysteries [?], so that he was high-king over the host as it went over the plain of Moab.
The King who spoke to Joshua, a perfect word: 'Go to the help of the great host; meet bravely, a clear deed, the fierce battles of the heathen.'
'Set the hosts in their ranks; be around them on every side. Rude, barbarous bands will not withstand your noble face.'
The King who gave a special sound condition [?] to the noble children of Abraham: they were without sickness and without want while Joshua was in command.
Joshua, with lawful command, put them in a fine, noble encampment [?] over the plains of Moab, a goodly course, as far as the stream of the excellent Jordan.
Sixty thousand along the way, fifteen thousand with a full hundred, a hundred thousand and a great noble seven [?] on each side of the great host.
Joshua divided the host into three, a perfect saying, without fault, so that no outsider could attack them, equally strong as they were made strong.
Even if the hosts of all four quarters were to fill the plain against them, floods of valour, before their peoples they would be routed in many thousands, up to heaven [?].
The King who made smooth for them a safe path to reach the land of Canaan: with dry feet, a most wondrous tale, they went over the stream of Jordan.
They brought with them out of the stream, to be arranged and set in order by the host, a great stone for each tribe. It was a heavy enough load.
King before the elements, a perfect saying; a King who will still be after the everlasting Judgement; a King above the sun, bright is what he loved; the radiant King who ordained. King.
The King who filled the excellent children of Israel with vigorous strength, so that they reached their borders in the plains around Jericho.
After that, having gathered their great wealth, the fierce host set up their camps, the number of their [?] ... [?], around the chief city.
Seven strong, very great walls, surely and boldly, surrounded the city, which was adorned with colours to withstand many battles.
The host sounded seven trumpets around the city as they went around it, so that a wall melted each day of a week, a clear might.
The people of the city with their [?], many, all of them, many thousands, went under the edge of the sword by the will of God, who overthrows every valour.
Except only Rahab, wonderful in deeds, none of the strong or the wretched escaped the heavy vengeance; not a single man of the great hosts got away.

The King who brought them onto sound, fruitful lands out of vast, great deserts, a splendid course without fear after a long way, the glorious King who filled them with health. The King who filled them with vigorous strength.
The seven warlike peoples of Canaan gathered a strong mass of troops [?], with a steady, strong array, to fight against the people of God.
The children of Canaan made battle against God's people. It was harshly shaped, so that they were overthrown with sorrowful force in the territories of the land of Beth-horon.
When Joshua raised his two hands to the Lord of holy, shining heaven, the grim battle would break upon the seven peoples of Canaan.
When his two hands grew weary from keeping the cross-vigil, a keen strength, Joshua would let them down to his side. Then there was a true rout of his own people.
The leaders of the host made a clever plan with pure victory: they set strong, very great stones under his hands.
After that the battle broke and the slaughter scattered. None of them remained, the saying is certain, so that all were cast into red slaughter.
So the seven kings were killed with their hosts, a countless band, every single man alive [?], ... [?], of the race of the children of Canaan.
The sun shone for the host on the western side, over Gibeon. It did not move; it stayed at rest for the space of two full, fair days.
The beloved light stayed still at God's command from holy heaven. The men of the host of Canaan died together; they did not stir from the one place.
What God did from heaven in miracles, in wonders and in glorious deeds at the time of the battle cannot be told [?]. They are beyond counting.

The seven famous kings, on a red-glowing course, with fierce fighting, with great hosts, with victories, with battles, with strength and power, gathered peoples and lands. They gathered a strong [?] band [?] of hills [?].
Joshua divided (a famous tale) among the hosts of the children of Israel, in twelve portions, with a bold clamour [?], the seven chief peoples of Canaan.
Over the division of the land they idly [?] made much contention, so that it was the casting of lots that settled it among the very great tribes.
As it is remembered from long ago, the first lot went to the bands of Benjamin. In these divisions, by its course [?], the second went to Simeon.
The third falls, by a just warlike deed [?], to the prosperous seed of Zebulun. The fourth, a deed of rank, went to the pure, bright offspring of Issachar.
The fifth lot, a keen deed, went to the pure host of the race of Asher. The sixth lot after that [?] went to the famous offspring of Naphtali.
The seventh lot, a pure and complete lot after a just division, went to Dan. The eighth, pure and bright [?], a fine deed, went to the wonderful race of Ephraim.
The ninth went to Gad without reproach, with valour, beside the river in the south-east. The tenth lot went to Judah by his will [?]. The choice portion went to Reuben.
The tribe of Manasseh, of thousands of kinds [?], was divided into parts [?]. Beside the river to the south it got a hold; the other half was in the north beside Ephraim.
The tribe of Levi, with lines of story [?], was throughout the lands of the children of Israel, without warfare [?], with clear rank, for freedom [?] and for priesthood.
The holy church with its Ark was set in one place, to spread [?] whole, special strength and for the meeting [?] of their assembly.
Among the dwellings of the gentle hosts, Joshua made a clear division of the seven chief peoples of fair Canaan, sound, with their subject peoples. Joshua divided (a famous tale).
The tribe of Judah, the tribe of gentle Simeon, and the tribe of Benjamin lay north-west from the strong, shallow river to the borders of the Tyrrhenian Sea.
The half-tribe of Manasseh without disgrace, the tribe of Ephraim and the tribe of Issachar lay to the north, straight along the river, to dwell and to settle.
The tribe of Naphtali (a famous tale) and the delightful tribe of Asher won their victory in every way [?]. They stretched north-east from the river.
The tribe of Zebulun, which strikes down wrath [?], and the tribe of Dan of the bright-red flame placed their settlement [?] beside bright, pure water [?], north-east from the Sea of Galilee.
The tribe of Reuben, the tribe of Gad that was not narrow [?], and the half-tribe of Manasseh were assigned land beside the river to the south-east. Their beauty [?] was not feeble.
On the eastern side of the tribe of Dan stretch the ranges of Mount Lebanon, beside the princely strength [?] of the host that strikes [?] the bridle [?], at the border of all Israel.
Annaneos, a cry that is not narrow [?]; Sidarios, a red kingdom [?]; Echeos, purity without horror [?]: these are the three hosts [?] [peaks?] of the mountains of Lebanon.
Hebron, Gassear, great Masheal, Gibeah, Gesseon and Gilead are six cities that all the children of Israel dwell in, I have related [?].

The King who brought them through the strong wilderness into the river Jordan, the generous and just King who took them [?], apportioned to them every single tribe. The tribe of Judah, the tribe of gentle Simeon.
The King who raised them by his might from the dreadful bondage of Egypt is the one who settled them, a sound track [?], on the borders of the children of Canaan.
Over the Philistines, above every plain [?], over Nathsared [?], over the Galaib [?], over Arabia with its host, over Moab and over Ammon.
Over the white [?] lands of Abethib [?], over the paths of the Samaritans, over the plains, without sorrow, [?] around the river Jordan.
Over Zeeb, over Zebah, a splendid race, over Zalmunna, over Ishmael, over Mount Zion, with paths of grace [?], over Gilead, over Jehoshaphat.
Over Amalek above every throng, over Assyria and over Tyre, over gentle Midian, in pure manner, over Kishon, over Sisera.
Over the sons of Lot, with bright lines, over Edom, over Idumea, over the Amorites, a splendid course, over Gebal and over Bashan.
Over the land of Gath, over dark [?] Carmel, over Terebinth, over Tabor, over Gilgal, which God loved, over the plain of Mesopotamia.
Over the lands of the whole [?] nations; Zelophehad, against the onset of heavy hosts [?]; Mahlah, Milcah, splendid Hoglah, Noah [Micha] and wave-white Tirzah.
Over the valley of Mamre, a wondrous saying, the first dwelling of Abraham, over Sihon, sound [?] of the hosts, over Samaria, over Beth-horon.
Over Jericho of lofty [?] hosts, over pure Gilboa [?], over Gibeon, over the stream of Kidron without falsehood, over the wondrous Mount of Olives.
Every strong people, it is certain, without sorrow, the sons of Israel took possession of: by the will of God, a warlike deed without sin, they spread out across the world.
From noble Alexandria, from the south, from all Africa, northward to the border of Media and Persia, they ruled its neighbouring lands.
On the western side, keen without sorrow, from the great shore of the Tyrrhene Sea, they [?] eastward to the noble border of the Euphrates.
My God, swift at the smooth course [?], a king who can shatter thunder, a king with [?] a fair body [?], a king without father who raised them up. A king who raised them up through his strength.
The King who freed them, above every wall, in every conflict, a very keen course, so that neither battle nor plunder overcame them while Joshua was their leader.
He broke thirty hard battles, he carried off their triumph in pure victory, with a multitude of lords, [?], with thirty very illustrious over-kings.
When Joshua son of Nun died, their leader of heavy-tower desires [?], they each went their own way [?]; they rejected their Lord.
A hundred and twenty years was the age of Joshua son of Nun before death, until he was buried, [?], in Timnath [Tamara], on the mountain of Ephraim.
The King who was before the world's [?], who made the courses of the bright stars, who fashioned every rank in a body [?], the glorious King who freed them. The King who freed them above every wall.
When they parted, a clear deed, from the worship of the King of holy heaven, a plague of destruction overwhelmed them; he put them under every heavy vengeance.
Fierce Cushan, bloodiest of every champion, leader of Mesopotamia, put them without stint [?] into subjection, into bondage, for service.
Eight years were they, a splendid burden, in dark bondage to Cushan, until wondrous, renowned Othniel [Nathanel] delivered them from him through his might.
Bright Eglon, king of the Moabites, enslaved them fully enough, until Ehud brought them away from him by battle, by force, after killing him.
Sisera and Jabin enslaved them by their might, until Deborah and Barak freed them from every distress.
Amalek and Midian oppressed them vehemently; fair Gideon gloriously freed them with the help of God from holy heaven.
To him the abundant flame was shown out of the very great bright rock; for him a shower fell on the pure fleece while there was drought on the earth.
He slew sixty thousand men with three hundred, a fierce deed, and in it Oreb died, and Zalmunna, Zeeb and Zebah.

The children of Israel were in captivity and bondage, held in contempt, without victory, without strength, without [?] vigour, until they were parted from it by the king we have spoken of. From then on they were parted from it, a clear deed.
The judgments of Gideon, pure and wise. Of his seventy sons (ten and three score), their brother Abimelech slew all but one man. It was woeful.
But the youngest escaped from him, Jotham (Ionas), [?] of the great hosts. It was a sad deed, hard for the people of the fort [?]: he slew them on one stone.
Many leaders from each tribe, who were not steadfast in a single succession: Tola, Jair, young Jephthah, Ibzan, Abigilon [?].
The king who gave them up to death [?], three nines of them and three score, on one stone [?], fair fame. It is there their judgments were given. The judgments of Gideon, pure and wise.
Of the tribe of Dan, of swift renown, was born sound Samson, famous, of noble birth, son of Manoah, a diadem of the great prowess of princes, of the wondrous race of Abraham.
He went out from his father, since he was handsome and proud, and took a haughty wife from the peoples of the Philistines. It was a sad deed.
No one can recount without fault [?] the deeds of red-speared Samson. As far as he could, he brought great swiftness to every harm through tricks.
Through the host of foxes, a clear track, came the burning of the vineyards [?]; through the hard jawbone a thousand of the great host perished.
Through the [?] ... a pure pledge, through the hard riddle, a fair contest, through the doors, a profitable feat,
when he carried them off from their place to break the city. Mighty through his threefold strength [?], through his ravaging, without weakness [?], of the hosts of every fort.
The great, bright, kingly, gracious King worked a very swift miracle when sound, strong Samson of the red [?] strokes was slaughtering the hosts.
When he was thirsty on the slope, slaying in the blood-red battle, God gave him a drink of pure water out of the tooth.
He betrayed himself, a sad case, through the shaving of his great mane. His destruction afterwards was together with the good men [?] in one union [?].

Samson, the plunderer [?] and slayer of hosts, was a prince of renown [?], son of Manoah. No one like him was found in the time in which he was born. Of the tribe of Dan, of swift renown, was he born.
A revered and splendid offspring was born: young Samuel, pure and very modest, son of Elkanah, whose word was pure, and son of Hannah of [?] judgment.
Elkanah, of bounded [?] grip, was from Ramathaim on Mount Ephraim. Hannah was his wife, with victory, the special mother of Samuel.
He was a sage, a venerable priest, noble, gentle, devout, pure and fair. He was a humble, innocent, chaste prophet, for teaching the great hosts.
