The King afterwards took vengeance on Eli and his sons. After that Samuel, in ranks of discipline, was a chief priest as well as a prophet.
From the time of Joshua [?], with victory, to the time of dear Samuel, there was none of them who equalled him as chief prophet or chief leader.

The King raised him up, with thousands of tales, over the lands of the sons of Israel. From the north he was a strong man [?], he was good; a revered offspring was born. A revered and splendid offspring was born.
Dagon was haughty and swift [?] about his idol [?] on his course [?], when the ark of God was brought to him before warriors, after slaughters, after the main roads [?].
When vengeance was mightily brought on the lands of the sons of Israel, at the end of Eli and his children, they all went to their destruction.
When thirty thousand armed men of them fell in the battle, including the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas.
The Philistines carried the ark off with them, as had befallen them, with ranks of bright voices [?], with fierceness, to the great, tearful temple of Dagon.
When the ark of the mighty Lord reached Dagon in his house, it ground the god to meal in the dust; it changed his form in a single hour.
Many thousands of them fell, a lively band, a harsh din; God slew them, a clear uproar, because they had seized the ark.
Even those of them who did not die, He tormented them with disgrace; their insides [?] came out of them, a clear sign, so that they were not [?].
The ark of the king of bright kingship, of the great Lord of holy-shining heaven, was there in glowing honour [?] for seven fair, full months.
The ark was lifted with grace onto two cows without [?], with their calves shut away in captivity; the cows were fair and both in milk.
Fitting offerings were put with the ark by them, as had befallen them: images of mice [?], images of the anuses (the emerods), of red gold.
The King who directed the two cows to the ark without error, along the right road (finish the tale!), until it came to rest at [?].
There were people at a feast there, whose name was Beth-shemesh; they gathered, a bright company, to gaze at the ark.
But of the host, a dear gathering, that came to gaze at it, sixty men of fierce renown among them died at once.
After that, fifty thousand of the great host died, a fresh [?], of the bright-coloured people, a bright folk, around the city of the Beth-shemeshites.
The Beth-shemeshites sent word to the hosts of the sons of Israel that their host should come quickly for the ark.
The peoples came to it, fair and equally swift, to welcome it without pride, the ark of the mighty King.
After that they brought the ark itself to the rock of Abel, because [?] it shaped every battle [?], to the house of Abinadab.
Eleazar of royal grace, of the race of Abinadab, a fair priest (a clear matter), was the priest of the ark.
The wondrous ark, of many glories, in the dwelling of Abinadab, stayed for twenty sweet years in the territory of Kiriath-jearim.

Until the King of the strong world crushed him [?] and overthrew him through his equally strong [?]. He was stout and goodly [?] for battle; he was spirited and he was proud. He was proud against swift Dagon.
From then the pure ark went across the great lands, across the great territory of the sons of Israel, as far as the sea [?]; they gathered in one assembly.
To drive the idols of [?] out of the lands of the sons of Israel, they gathered in ranks across the valleys until they were all at Mizpah.
Samuel spoke, an anxious message, to the angry host of Israel: 'Vengeance will overtake you on every plain for your wicked idols.'
'If you do not quickly put away from you your many great, proud idols, surely sharp vengeance will overtake you from the King of noble, holy-bright heaven.'
The sons of Israel obeyed God in every place before the One of fair renown; after that they bowed down to dear God without worshipping idols.
Then it was truly reported to the hosts of the Philistines, and they came against them with their army as far as Mizpah.
The sons of Israel said, in agitation, a fresh course [?]: 'Pray to the mighty Lord that victory in the battle may be ours.'
Through grace Samuel made an offering and prayed earnestly to the King of cloudy heaven on behalf of the children of Israel.
The King who brought back the ark, who carried it over every great wall, into every place, every land, routed the Philistines, leaving them without protection.

The King who brought vengeance on the hosts of the Philistines, leaving them without protection, on every shore where the ark imposed its constraint [?]; from then on it arrived. From then on the whole ark arrived.
Joel and Abijah, of noble victory, two distinguished, stately sons of Samuel, were not concealed [?] in their fame; they were judges of the children of Israel.
They were unlike [?] others in mean deeds, in false judgement, in false witness; the great hosts of the children of Israel, a strong flood, were displeased with them.
In throngs of tribes and assemblies, a bright flood, from Dan to Beersheba, they came to Samuel at the fort, to Ramah.
They begged of God, a full cry, and they begged of Samuel, for battles, for vigour, for strength, that they might not be without a single king.
Samuel asked them in answer: 'Why do you reject [?] God, your Lord? Your King, the high king of holy and noble heaven, is better than every glorious king.'
'[?] You have broken the clear law [?] through your disobedience, because of your wickedness without [?], O good people of Israel!'
After that the host spoke its manly answer to Samuel: 'For the sake of great strength of famous troops we will not be without a human king.'
The prophet Samuel ordained Saul son of Kish, with pure fighting [?], for noble lofty strength, a dear renown, as sole king [?] noble.
From then Saul took the red kingship, eagerly, with fiery nobility [?]; the wondrous tribes of Jacob were filled with valour and glory.
So that they would not be without a glorious king, they all asked for it in a single assembly: they hated Abijah and Joel, with thousands of tales. Joel, Abijah, of noble victory.
Nahash king of Ammon, a famous saying, imposed constraint on the host of Gilead, so that he took the firm right eyes out of their fair heads.
He enslaved them along with their clans, a cruel [?] deed under black showers [?], with strong, heavy [?] tributes, with hides of swift, bright-backed beasts.
The host of Gilead asked Nahash plainly for a truce of a week, to see whether they could find anyone at all under heaven to defend them.
They sent their sorrowful message to Saul and to Samuel, to see whether they could find full strength that would protect them against the host of Ammon.
After that Saul set out on the road with six hundred thousand [?], without weakness, and thirty thousand splendid men of the hosts of fierce Judah.
He defeated Nahash, with complete slaughter, in a brave and full battle; that was his first bright victory after he took the kingship.
Saul went, with choice battalions, to the [?] peoples of Ammon; a tower of [?] lords, the support of hosts, he hemmed in Nahash king of Ammon. Nahash king of Ammon, a famous saying.
He won another strong victory, gained over the great hosts, with abundance of [?], in splendid manner, by Saul and by Jonathan.
The hosts of the fierce, very hard Philistines came against them, not for forgiveness but for battle, to destroy them and plunder them swiftly.
To avenge Nahash, renowned in fighting, on Saul and on the host of Gilead, with sharp battle full of captives [?], a complete deed, in venomous alliance with Ammon.
When the fiery throng of the Philistines was counted, a fiery defence: thirty thousand chariot-warriors of battle and six thousand armed men.
The full number of his household went swiftly, a keen deed, against their enemies: two thousand with Saul, unharmed, and a thousand with Jonathan.
So that they attacked the hosts of the Philistines and of the Ammonites, and they inflicted a complete [?], fierce slaughter on Ammon and on the Philistines.
When the son of Kish had taken the kingship, he broke a host of many thousands; he pursued them after a clear victory, and he won another victory. Another mighty victory he achieved.
Once there came from their land the fierce war-bands of the Philistines, those hosts, [?] against the prince [?], to destroy the sons of Israel.
The number of their host, a track without fault [?], in ranks from the north, a heavy throng [?]: seven thousand men, better than any in valour, with arms, with weapons.
There gathered, a mighty will [?], the great hosts of the sons of Israel, fearful and sorrowful [?] [?], until they were all in one assembly.
My holy, noble King spoke to Jonathan, above everyone else, telling him to go after due preparation [?] to see the host of the Philistines.
Jonathan went apart, alone with his armour-bearer, and he killed of them, [?], twenty thousand very strong men.
The King who took vengeance, a splendid din [?], laid them low [?] before Jonathan, from Michmash, with thousands of hosts, to the border of wrathful Achilon [Aijalon?].
Not by multitudes of men, [?] shoulders, with bright blades, a fierce feat of arms [?], did a strong, mighty lord save them, but my kingly, star-bright [?] King.

They took their course, a road that divided [?] the hosts, [?] of the children of Jacob; they bore it with strength, with the protection of valour [?]. Once they came from their land. Once they came from their land.
The King spoke to Samuel, joyful [?], that he should tell Saul to go with the full number of his lordly host, without fail [?], to plunder Amalek.
He was not to bring away with him their cloaks, their clothing, nor their gold, nor their silver; he was to cast it all to the ground; both woman and man, let it be a red slaughter.
Without sparing cattle, without sparing the fair horse-herd, or the herds of swine all together, so that they would bring home with them no herds of goats or of sheep.
After that Saul went against all the warriors [?] he found, and he slew them with [?] [?] vengeances, red-backed demons [?].
Three hundred thousand, good is the tale, of the hosts of the sons of Israel, and ten thousand, great the fame, of the warriors of the tribe of Judah.
Saul, among the hosts, disobeyed what Samuel had said: he brought with him the produce of the land of the lords, and he brought the king of Amalek.
Choice [?] was the debt that was paid to Agag, to Amalek; not soft [?] is the lasting might of the lordly King who spoke to Samuel. The King spoke to Samuel, joyful [?].
God, divine, distinguished, very great, was at odds with Saul the healthy, because Agag was spared, a clear saying, and because he disobeyed His command.
Samuel went without delay to Agag, king of Amalek; he decreed his fitting death by the sword in Gilgal.
The King spoke a hidden, very gentle message to Samuel the prophet: 'In the place of Saul, a track of peace [?], perform the anointing of David.'
The King chose, a bright onset [?], David, the good son of Jesse; when he was a sound boy of seven years he gave counsel of equal sense [?].
The King of the world, melodious, lasting His strength, for His keen hardness [?], for His renowned strength, [?] [?] except that He was angry, was at odds. At odds with Saul the healthy.
The King who brought Abimelech past the host to Moab, with his wife and his two sons, fair the fame, when he went from Bethlehem of Judah.
Abimelech, without seed of sorrow [?]; Naomi, Mahlon, Chilion, Orpah with vigour [?], a feast of generosity, and Ruth the Moabitess.
Fair Ruth the Moabitess went a long journey with Naomi, with thousands of fame [?], until she reached Bethlehem of Judah.
After that she was joined to Boaz son of Salmon; it was no unsteady union [?]: from him, after a time, was born a son whose name was Obed.
Salmon the sound, in ranks of wisdom [?], was a descendant of Perez; Perez of pure [?] nurture, a bright deed, was the son of Tamar and Judah.
Ruth was the mother of Obed, a clear saying; Obed was the father of Jesse; Jesse, without disrespect [?] or loss [?], was the true father of David.
David, chosen one of bright fame, was once herding; a lion, full of fury, came upon him and carried off a sheep from his flocks.
The lion ran on ahead of all, with David alone after it, through the [?] of his fair spirit [?], until he overtook the lion.
Bold David overcame the lion of fierce fighting, and through his bravery, openly, he brought the sheep out of its gullet.
David and the fiercely fighting lion waged a fierce struggle: David was the stronger, he who overran [?] territory, with the help of the High King. The King who brought them past the host.
The fierce peoples of the Philistines gathered a long hosting, with many victories (a great tale), against the peoples of the sons of Israel.
With a multitude of spears and hosts, with the might of red-sworded champions: strong was the plan they made, to plunder them and to destroy them.
To destroy the [?] throng, their women and their dearly loved sons, to drive them from their territories (a proper course), to [?] their memory.
The huge, arrogant host marched without sorrow to the battle; they set up a loud [?], bright camp in the middle of the Valley of the Terebinth.
Both near and far, they all made a common expedition; the hosts, without affection [?], [?] of array, gathered from their territories. They gathered a long hosting.
They brought with them a wrathful champion whose name was Goliath, of rough deeds: he was not a pleasant or comely man of the host; he was a grim, huge [?].
A churlish, mad, stammering cur [?], with a great deal of clothing all about him; his height, of vast shape, was seven cubits and [?].
A breastplate about him, rough in form, for combat and for battle; fifty hundred ounces was its weight.
The blade of his spear, before every throng, was seven hundred ounces of iron, with a fair shaft, finished and shapely, as thick as the beam of an ox-yoke.
His greaves were of pure bronze from his knees to the ground; a helmet of grey iron was fashioned about the very crown of his head.
A sharp, rough sword in his grasp, the size of a sword like a strong weaver's beam; a shield on his left side, not hidden, which was broader than an ox-hide.
Every day he had a man of the hosts of the sons of Israel in distress [?]; not one man of them was found alone who would withstand him because of his weaponry.
Hideous Goliath, of bright valour, bold against heavy hosts, in contest — his rule was not pleasant — he was a grim champion whom they brought. They brought with them a wrathful champion.
Though many of the host of the children of Israel were strong, trembling seized them, [?], before sharp, rough-bearded Goliath.
He put them in [?] around [?]; he constrained them without pride and without fighting [?]; a loud din he made beyond every gathering; a champion each day to destroy them [?].
Sorrow filled, anger seized long-flanked, red-speared Saul; a man each day by him (though it was [?]) was killed of his good men.
Saul son of Kish, valiant and sharp, rightful king of the children of Israel, promised his daughter without fail to the one man who would slay him.
He put them into anxiety, [?] for a while, without sure protection for their [?]; wretched, rough, without any [?], though they were very many. Though many of the host.
David then came, the youngest of the children of Jesse, at that time from his home to the host, with provisions for his brothers.
He heard the lament, with cries rising to the clouds, that was on the hosts of Israel: a combat of two men without battle, and each day one man of them was killed.
David asked openly among the people, of his brothers: 'What reward or what payment does the king give to the man who would kill him?'
With lasting, ever-smooth words, the brothers told David, without any falsehood [?], how fully Saul had promised it.
Saul son of Kish had promised his daughter, without fault or breach of law [?], together with every good thing he could give, to the one man who would slay him.
David, fitting [?] and eager for valour, was at that time a leader of hosts, pure in psalms; it was hard to look upon his face at the time when he came. Thus David came.
'I will go,' said David, without sorrow, 'to Saul, king of Israel, so that he may give me the girl openly if I kill the champion.'
His friends tried every way of advising him, to rebuke him: to his brothers it seemed dangerous to speak of it or even to think of it.
David spoke boldly before the good people of Israel: 'I will slay that man of the host, and let his reward be given to me.'
Then Saul promised David, without dispute, a girl for him — certain tidings — and his favour above the children of Israel.
'A guarantee for it, pure-voiced one [?], O righteous, triumphant son of Kish! Without dishonouring the compact in any way, to confirm it truly.'
'You shall have from me the guarantee of the host, under the special anointing [?] of Samuel, as the power of thought raised me [?] under my own superiority of true sovereignty.'
'The honour of Joseph above all, of Moses, of Jacob and of Jesse; and lastly an honour above every assembly, nobler than theirs: the God of Abraham.'
'From me to you, at every assembly, a clear proclamation, into your hand, O son of Jesse, whatever hardship you may undergo, provided only that you kill the champion.'
'I will kill Goliath, a bright deed; it will be the bond of friendship; my might will be a boast above him [?]; at my king's will I will go.' 'I will go,' said David, without sorrow.
David went to meet that man without a mail-coat, in swift array, without spear, without shield, [?], without dark sword, without helmet.
He took five flawless stones from the shore of the great stream; he set himself toward victory ... [?] in his pouch [?], terrible [?].
He took one stone of them — it was a sharp deed — and hurled it from him into the air; it struck Goliath on the crown of his head, so that it reached his brain.
After that David came to him and took from him his own sword, and brought his head away through fierce struggle [?], so that it was set before Saul.

David, without guilt [?], won victory from the holy, victorious King of heaven; not pitiful was the due before his face [?]; swiftly he went without a mail-coat. He went without a mail-coat, in swift array.
The two hosts rose up for the gory, red-sworded battle, to reach one another head to head, to smite one another firmly.
At the onset of the grim, clamorous warriors, of the hard champions, with the number of the swift, fiery throng, they were for a while [?] fighting one another with swords.
The King made an assault upon the battle before swift, furious David, so that the battle was broken, without fail, upon the host of the joyful [?] Philistines.
There was rough gore over pale bodies in the battle of the Valley of the Terebinth, so that of them there fell — a clear crash — six men, fifty and five thousand [?].
The hosts of the Philistines in fury [?] and the hosts of the children of Israel — not long until the onset of valour — rose up in a swift gathering. The two hosts rose up.
When the battle was broken before David with great grace, the host said sharply: 'He is far better than Saul.'
David was praised, with a noise of choirs [?], above Saul and above the great host. Sweet was the clear, bright song of the Hebrew maidens.
While only a thousand fell to Saul and his hosts, ten thousand, a great and heavy slaughter, fell to David.
David's band [?], pure in strength, faced an army beyond counting: four [?] useful champions on behalf of friends and companions [?].
After that, by victorious might, he won Saul's daughter from [?] the ranks of hosts: great Michal, greater than anyone in purity [?], before the face [?] of good people.
He slew Goliath, a warlike [?] heap [?], so that the host was praising him greatly. The bloody son with his hand ... [?] a fierce contest [?] ... with him in sight [?].

The hosts of the kings, with the might of a lord, gathered around the high king. Each of them was glad that he had gone to the battle from the place where the battle broke. From the place where the battle broke.
David and Jonathan made a whole peace according to God's rule, a fair arrangement, for the whole length of their lives.
Jonathan truly gave David his own equipment: clothing fit for gracious honour, and spear, shield and sword.
They settled a holy covenant, so that there would be no meeting in war, whether for good or ill, for ever, between Saul and David.
Michal wished, without failing her brother, her chief [?], that Jonathan and David should be in friendship without end.
David was in glory, rightly in rank beside Jonathan, often in honour. Once, at a dangerous time [?], he was trying to go to Saul.
Michal, true joy [?], gave David prudent counsel: 'Do not go, because of slippery tidings, to the wise king of Israel.'
'Do not go to him [?], bright face [?], to the son of Kish, without [?] ... It would be foolish not to heed counsel. Do not put your trust in Saul.'
Saul went against the new peace, quickly, to David's house, to seize David there without warning, without preparation.
When he came, a mighty troop, the bloody king of the children of Israel, then David, with a keen noise [?], went out on the path to [?] Saul.
Saul arrayed the whole line around David's house with great terror; like a serpent, in bright [?] battle, he closed around the city of the son of Jesse.
When Michal heard the news that the host had set out toward the house, she gathered a heap [?] of the linen cloths and the wraps [?].
She arranged them, that was the cunning deed, her fair, curly, truly noble ... [?]; she pleasantly set the locks [?] all around the pillow.
So she quickly made a likeness of the man from them in the bed [?], as was his custom to lie always under his covering [?].
Saul the noble-born, of clear command, called from outside the door. He spoke a clear word [?]: 'Is the son of Jesse in there?'
Michal said in a gentle voice to Saul, to calm him: 'Unless it is an omen [?] of your battle, welcome is the coming of a good father.'
'O Michal, wanton [?], spirited, bright, ... [?], shapely, let him come out under ... [?], your many ... [?], your foster-brother.'
'What you seek, O son of Kish, O pillar of valour, without neglect [?], is here, without any clear outcry [?], between your daughter's two hands.'
'Even if he is in your hand, bright ... [?], the evil son of splendid Jesse, you will not protect him against my sharp attack, O daughter of Ahinoam!'
'Whatever you hate most, O armed king of Israel, let it come before your vengeance at my word [?]; it is not kingly of you to violate me.'
'O Michal, wild, spirited and beautiful, O descendant of nimble Athemas [?], you will not have as your beloved, to your bitter sorrow [?], the royal heir of the sons of Israel.'
'O son of Kish, with your fierce deeds, do not break [?]; do not drown through mighty [?] contention the leader in the warfare of Israel.'
'Since the son of Jesse has come to meet me in a bright onslaught, O warlike woman of the Féni, he will not be a heart-loving husband to you.'
'O son of Kish, practised in deeds, a bright deed, do not lie in wait for the son of Jesse; desist from your bright, habitual destroying [?]; do not wrong your good daughter.'
'Do not wrong noble Jonathan of the customary valour, who has stood firm [?]; without evil, without malice, without ruin, he has made friendship with David.'
'Do not wrong fair Samuel the prophet, who held a proud, holy, delightful rank; do not wrong, without falsehood, the voice of Moses, Joseph and Jacob.'
'Do not break the fighting of nobles or of warriors, nor the honour of the truly wise men; do not make a practice of anything of which an ill tale will be told [?]; do not wrong the God of Israel.'
'Though I were given in exchange for him [?], O woman, a hundred ounces of red gold, for valour, prowess or bright generosity [?], I would not spare the son of Jesse.'
'God from heaven has saved him, the fair, pure noble without contention, of noble deeds [?], without being held in locks [?]; he has gone from you on this occasion.'
Michal of the battles [?] held him back from going after David, until David, in a course of flight, reached far into one of the wildernesses.
After that David and Jonathan met without torment, and they settled, without tears or sorrow, their everlasting friendship for ever.
Their unity always in every way, their trust without separation, was established before worthy witnesses of valour according to oaths. They made a complete peace.
Once David was in the royal house, with his back to the wall, before the king, in the pleasant company of the gathered throngs [?], sitting together with Jonathan.
The master of song, of beautiful form, with gentle music, was playing his sweet-stringed timpán for the king and for the host, without grievous affliction.
David of the graces, a noble course, was the foundation of a truly holy sovereignty; the psalm-like strain [?] was a wonderful, marvellous music.
It was a gentle sound in every respect, in its form, its music and its harmony, to the noble, very attentive [?], peaceful host; sweet to them was listening to David.
Though it was entertainment for everyone through the ages, a great prophecy, the Devil, by a smooth path, went past the host into Saul.
Saul hurled the spear at David in the royal house; the bright, sharp-pointed spear stuck [?] through the hard board beside his head.
The host inside rose up; a cry went up from the household: everyone thought the king's spear had gone through David's middle.
Noble Jonathan rose up and made a very fierce, powerful dash, and escorted David, a bright rush, away to one of the forests.
He fought fiercely and powerfully against his father, against the high king; grief seized him, his appearance changed, because of the wrong done to him [David].
Michal waged a sharp quarrel with Saul and with Ahinoam; she was not restrained in her fight; she was sorrowful, she was very contentious.
The host poured sharp words on the red-faced king, on Saul, because he had gone without making peace, wronging David.
Saul's son, of slaughtering battle-deeds, the fierce rousing of a lion, saved his kinsman by marriage, his foster-brother, without the gloom of captivity.

The King who protected him on the plain from the lion, without his being seen [?], is the one who saved him, without the king's thanks, in the seat where David was. David was with his back to the wall.
David, the splendid warrior, made a plan with Jonathan to leave openly, away from fierce violence, so that he would no longer be in Saul's household.
Jonathan said to him: 'Do not neglect this. Wait here for my call for a while, at the stone whose name is Ephel [Ezel].'
'Then I may find out whether the high king's mind toward you is set on good peace, or whether the hard-fighting warrior of the battles [?] is eager to harm you.'
'A sign will come to you from me, and it will be a good omen for your fair victory [?]: either it goes ahead of you (a clear, keen rule) or it falls behind you again.'
'I will shoot a swift arrow from me, keen [?] toward your pure companion [?]. As far as it reaches, the course of good fortune [?], even if it is seen far off.'
'If it goes far without fail [?], take the step that settles your full welfare [that is, flee]. If it does not go far, it is a special sign that you may come quickly to the royal house.'
Jonathan went in to the king and his household, and sat down in his seat as royal heir without showing any grief.
Saul eagerly [?] asked Jonathan for news of David: 'Where is he, the [?] warrior who fights battles as bold as any?'
'Where outside is the wicked son of fierce Jesse? He has not come before the company here on any of these days.'
Jonathan, the splendid warrior, gave the king the glorious [?] answer in the royal house: 'The warrior has gone from his home, without deceit [?], to Bethlehem of Judah.'
Saul said to the new company [?]: 'Who in the host has not done me harm, when it is you who have done this, you wicked son of the harlot?'
Jonathan went out and stood on the city wall, as he always did without fail, to see whether he could catch sight of David.
Without grief he sent a strong shot from the wall out onto the rock. It was stately and well-shaped, a clear track, as a sign to be remembered.
'If anyone is at the stone yonder,' said Jonathan, who was not mean, 'let him get up [?] quickly and come to fetch it. The arrow has been let fly from him.'

The King who spread the noble canopy of heaven around the sides of the white-waved earth, and the keen sun with its beauty: every creature he made is subject to his will. David made, splendid warrior...
David, full of grace, went away with no spear, no shield and no sword, across rough hills. He had taken up valour [?], and he left his weapons in the royal house.
After that he went, in the guise of a servant [?], to Ahimelech the priest, and with him he ate a keen choice [?]: bright loaves prepared beforehand [the shewbread].
[?] about the needs of the body of clay [?], Abimelech questioned David. He asked in a fair manner: 'Are the people of your household pure?'
David gave true testimony in the presence of the high king: for three days and three nights he had not had intercourse with women [?].
The sword of Goliath had been in the sanctuary without glory and without prohibition [?], as a famous trophy before every host, after it had been given to Saul.
David said, though it was a lie: 'It is bad to go far without weapons. A vigorous rush on the king's errand brought me here in haste.'
It was no hardship for Ahimelech. He welcomed David and handed out to him the sword of Goliath, sharp and deadly.
An Idumean [Doeg] told the story to Saul, king of Israel: David and his people, it was a pity [?], had eaten Abimelech's food.
It is no wonder [?] that David found a welcome under discipline [?] among the company of priests, and he took Goliath's sword away with him without payment and without neglect.
Saul went at once [?], after being informed, and seized the people of the city. He openly slew the company of priests, eighty-five of them.
He slew them after the first onset of his conflict [?], in their vestments, with linen ephod, with treacherous speech [?], a boast thus [?], in the city whose name is Nob.
But one man of them escaped to the house of David: Abiathar, with his strength [?], son of Ahimelech the priest.
Saul hated David, great son of Jesse (a manifest deed), so that he commanded (a broad tale) that he should not be within the borders of Israel.
After the son of Kish had given David this command, he showed no neglect [?]; without concealment he went away and took his flight to Achish.
Everyone said before the king, at the time when David had come: 'Is this the pure champion David, king of the lands?'
'Is it of him that the host of the fierce, very wild maidens speaks: "David slew a full ten thousand, bitter Saul slew one thousand"?'
After that a sharp sickness seized him, against the hard [?] ... it was not very strong [?], so that his mind was disturbed and every kind of frenzy began.
So Achish said in his vexation (he did not esteem David): 'Take away from us, without honour, the violent, mad man.'
David went, with the numbers of his host, into the small lands of Moab, with the folk who were present, with [?] household, with his mother and his father.
After that he dwelt [?] in the south in Mizpah, in Moab; a famous strength: Mizpah became the chief dwelling of the true prince.
When he had entrusted his father before the host to the king of Moab — over Israel, many territories [?] — after that David came away. David went away, with abundance of graces.
Saul, after a time, in his vexation, did a disgrace to David, so that Michal was given for good [?] to Palti son of Laish.
His own household spoke clearly and eagerly to Saul: 'Someone will incur the displeasure of God for outraging the son of Jesse.'
'God will avenge it in every way on yourself, on your children, on your race, [?] David ... [?] for outraging my first household [?].'
The people, firm and strong, were troubled [?]; many were the cries of the sons of Israel; with battle-throngs after [?] ..., they were at enmity with Saul. Saul, after a time, in his vexation.
David was for a long time apart, under proclamation, under banishments, in wretched state, under [?] ..., in the wilderness of Mount Carmel.
In the woods of Ziph, with rows of spears, bright-skinned David wandered, and on Mount Zion as well, in the harsh wildernesses.
Six hundred fine warriors of pure valour, of young men for combat, were with David truly for [?] ...; that was his number in his exile.
A fair company of women, purple-clad and comely, with their ornaments of red gold; a throng of maidens, a throng of proper young men, for their service and their attendance.
For hunting, for chasing game willingly, without sluggishness, for full counsel, with their dreadful band free of sorrow, over the peoples of the sons of Israel.
Around Mount Carmel on every side, without harsh grip on their neighbours, he would often [?] meet [?] about the vast herds of Nabal.
Nabal in Carmel was famed for taking a hold in the neighbourhood [?]; a strong [?] above [?] the life of fame [?]; a dweller of the wildernesses.
Abigail, pure her conduct [?], wife of Nabal of Mount Carmel: a lasting treasure, a path not concealed, a shapely, fair, prudent woman.
His vast herds, without weakness, around Carmel on every single slope: a thousand goats for grazing, three thousand sheep.
Messengers went from David to his house, at the time of the shearing of sheep, to Nabal for a fitting reception, to ask him plainly [?] for a night's feast.
Because of his rudeness towards guests [?] and the narrowness of his mind, that Nabal of Mount Carmel refused [to give] even a single loaf.
Five wethers, two hundred loaves of good bread, two hundred dishes of figs, two skins of wine: after a peaceful journey [?], the woman brought these with her to David.
With four hundred fine young men along the roads, ready for combat, with armed force, David came to meet him, to kill Nabal.
The woman made David welcome, without any neglect: 'We have brought you these things; we do not fail [?] in honour towards you.'
'If you had not come to meet me,' said David to Nabal's wife, 'tomorrow, in his fair chamber, Nabal would have been lifeless.'
Nabal, venomous, fettered [?], withered, [?] suffered a stroke [?]: on the tenth day, a joyful day without wrong [?], Nabal was dead, alone.
After that David took, without delay [?], Abigail, Nabal's wife; God from heaven gave her to him, with wealth and with herds.
The King blessed David beyond all others, with a union of great dignity. For seven [?] David was an outlaw, unharmed, in the wildernesses where he was. David was a long time apart.
The Ziphites – they were not [?] hosts – told Saul: 'David the outlaw, it is likely he is hiding from you in our wildernesses, in our solitudes.'
Saul came – that was no small thing – with the whole of his host, with armed valour, for the fierce work of making battle, until he was at the edge of the wilderness.
He pitched a camp; it was a deed of equal strength, without neglect; he settled [?] along the courses of the paths on the plains of the sheep-flocks.
He found, before witnesses of his father [?], a cave in the lands of the wilderness; for a need of his body, in every way, he went into it to relieve himself [?].
David, with the lords who were his [?], was in the back of the cave, strong men around him in [?] a dark wood [?], with his band, with his company.
His own people said to David – a course without harm: 'As was promised to you, a time without betrayal, now it has been fulfilled.'
'What was promised long ago has been brought under your command; long has this victory been under [?] control; in this hour it has arrived.'
'Great is the gift from dear God to you, O bright-sided David! [?] your bitter enemy, who brought tribulation, [has come] under your hands.'
'Let your sharp bright sword be taken at your will, O son of Jesse! Let Saul, bitter and fierce, eager [?], not go out safe to an assembly of a sure host.'
David rose after that and restrained his people; it was [?] to cut Saul's garment.
He went himself, a deed of excellence, David of [?] form [?] … [?], and cut – a daring, hard deed – the garment that was on Saul.
When Saul went out of the cave to his household, he took to reviling [?], in a manner that was not pleasant [?], with the Ziphites. The Ziphites – they were not [?] hosts.
Bold, hard David came on a quiet night to Saul, and took his fitting [?] spear, along with a ridged cup of red gold.
The spear that was at the side of his head, together with the fair bright cup – David took them, with keen sharpness, from Saul himself.
Were it not for fear of God from bright heaven, [?] for every dear fair counsel, [?] the fierce attack [?], he would have taken Saul's head with him.
The doomed one made a dark [?] until he fell in the battle of Gilboa; there was no peaceful [?] seat for him from the night that David came. Bold, hard David came.
While dear David was an outlaw in the wilderness under protection, he was a neighbour, bright and clear, of Nabal of Mount Carmel.
Saul drove him out, the warrior of boastful [?] fame. He went off with his strong band, so he was not alone [?], into Gath until he reached Achish.
Achish, with bright raids, gave the city called Ziklag, with its land and lawful hills [?], to David as his chief dwelling [?].
Since swift David settled in Ziklag with his great honour, its name from then on has been 'splendid Ziklag of the Judeans'.
Once, when David went without delay [?] to join a hosting with Achish, a raiding party came after he had gone, and it plundered and burned Ziklag.
The host of the Philistines did not let David go far with them, for fear that David would turn against them [?] at the call of Achish [?].
'So that the son of Jesse son of Obed does not attack us in battle [?], strong David shall not go with us to battle against the host of Israel.'
God did not let dear David be guilty of that hosting, for that, among the ranks of hosts, was the time when Saul was killed.
When David afterwards went back from Achish with his hosts, he found his brown fortress after its plundering: Ziklag stripped bare after its burning.
Without house, without household, [?] clear sound, without treasure, without cattle, without a living person under the clouded sky to tell them a single piece of news.
Without women, without sons, great valour [?], without gold, without foreign silver; without respite from the sorrow that arose [?]. David's face was overcome [?].
David went after the host until he reached the brook Besor, and he found a man from the people of the expedition who had failed to keep up on the journey.
David gave him food, without treachery, to strengthen him. Since he was no longer weary, he guided David toward the host.
After that David went on with three hundred, a fierce deed; two hundred [?] still stayed behind, having failed to keep up on the march.
The great host was routed before David, and it was a true rout, so that they left behind all the goods of their plunder, without a single pledge [?].
The host took a share of the spoils after their bright, rough valour, without anything for those who had stayed behind, sitting truly at rest [?].
David, firm and strong, allowed them only a share of the spoils held in common, out of love and without grudging, so that it would be a rule forever.
When he went to splendid Achish he got goods with great love. With bright valour every deed of fame was done according to God's will while David lived. While David was mighty and dear [?].
Saul, ever wrathful [?] slayer of hosts, was anxious after Samuel's death, with [?] plundering, without holiness, without prophecy.
The son of Kish, without joys, endured [?] on the borders of the sons of Israel. A torrent of anxiety filled him, a clear sign, because of his persecution of the son of Jesse.
The son of Kish was in long warfare against David with his great honour, until the hosts of the very strong men of the Philistines came from their land.
He gathered the hosting of bright-armed Israel to fight [?] against them, with bright warriors [?], on the fair plains of Gilboa.
On the night before the bitter battle Saul was very anxious, for he did not know through his fortune [?] which side the great battle would break against.
After that Samuel came to Saul that night and said to him, words without treachery: 'You will be killed tomorrow;
'and your three sons, a just measure, because of your crime and your transgression, and a sad, vengeful, mighty slaughter on the wrathful host of Israel;
'and the high kingship of the sons of Israel has been taken away from your line [?]. Your path, to see it truly, God has given to David.'
The King who separates falsehood from truth, who restrains perversity, who purges untruth, inflicted his vengeance, a complete outcry, and carried out a supreme judgment on Saul.
At the time when the bright sun shone from every course around the earth, as was their custom to go to battle, each one took up his battle-gear.

They fought a battle long ago, a hundred deeds of valour; they pressed against warrior-bands, a troop of men. In the battle of Gilboa, with his host, Saul was then slain. Saul the persistent, slayer of hosts.
Saul son of Kish had seven of his own true offspring: four sons, a fitting great company, and three very pure daughters.
Malchishua, who was strong in hosts and sound, Ishvi, Ishbosheth, Jonathan, Brígente, merry Merab, and great-spirited Michal.
Ahinoam was their beautiful mother, the wondrous daughter of Ahimaaz; and Saul, with ranks of valour: they were not obscure [?]. Saul the persistent, slayer of hosts.
The seed of Saul, troubled in their course, over the wrathful children of Israel: none [?] refused them [?] except the tribe of Judah alone.
Abner, through a sharp ruling, gave the kingship to Ishbosheth son of Saul; over the ten tribes he obtained his will, in the stronghold of Benjamin.
After dissensions among them, the people of God were contentious over the high-kingship, without profit [?] upon every house [?]; they were not a wondrous united household.
He cast them down without mighty kingship, since Saul had outraged Samuel; concerning the stern dark strongholds [?], the seed of Saul were not prosperous. The seed of Saul, troubled in their course.
There was a fitting vengeance [?] of strife on the ungentle ten tribes, with a display of weakness upon them [?], in the time of Saul's children.
Every noble host struck them down; it pressed them under a dark shower [?]; harshly a round of captivity was driven upon them; every weakness surrounded them.

Every evil destroyed them at that time; every fault [?] assailed them without fierce victory; it drove them [?] from battle to battle [?]; at that time there was vengeance. There was a fitting vengeance [?].
David took, by clear will, the complete kingship of the Jews, after the glorious battle of fierce red cheeks [?] in which the host fell around Saul.
He dwelt in splendid Hebron; he dwelt in all of Hebron [?], over the tribe of Judah, without bright ... [?], for six months and seven years.
David, without seed of sorrow, sent a messenger to Ishbosheth son of Saul, so that there might be given to him (she is named noble) fair Michal, his first wife.
Ishbosheth son of Saul, without grief, who had taken the kingship of Israel, took Michal, though he disliked it, from Phaltiel son of Laish.
So that she was brought to David from him, 'for the sake of great and glorious Judah, so that he might thereafter be in alliance, always in their true unity.'
There was a rough game, a strong clamour, at the pool of Gibeon, between modest Abner son of Ner and nobly-reared Joab son of Zeruiah.
Twenty-four, clearly, of Benjamin and of Judah, in equal measure, without loss of renown, fell in the first encounter.
In the second fight, by count, which Benjamin raised, there fell, foot to foot, sixty over three hundred [?].
Thereafter the battle was broken against Abner and his hosts; Asahel son of Zeruiah, in ranks of tales, it was then that Abner killed him.
Joab, whose territory was just [?], leader of David's soldiery, son of Zeruiah, who was bright and keen [?] in combat, killed Abner in vengeance for him.
Baanah and Rechab, on a secret course, killed Ishbosheth son of Saul; in a short while [?] after his death they brought his head to David.
While David was over mighty Judah, before the kingship of the sons of Israel, in Hebron, ... [?], seven sons were born to David.
Amnon, who is the eldest, a perfect line; Chileab, Absalom, Adonijah, of pure generosity, Shephatiah and Esrom [Ithream?].
The King who gave the law of great Judah to godly, brown-faced David: with whole ranks, with hosts of peace, with honours David took it. David took it, a bright will.
They gathered an assembly, certain, without sorrow, the elders of the host of the sons of Israel; following the command of God, the protection of every peace, they came to David.
They gave the kingship, a bright course, to the wondrous son of Jesse, to David with his soldiers, over peoples, over many lands.
David took the kingship of every part of each territory completely, from Dan, according to the will of God, to the plain of the land of Beersheba.
For his form, his valour [?], his wisdom, for his nobility, for his esteem, there was before him in no place any other king who was more wonderful.

The number of his household, the number of his nobles, the count of his chiefs of high rank, the number of his whole host against outrage and plunder [?]: great was the assembly they gathered. They gathered an assembly, certain, without sorrow.
Thirty years, without folly of strength, by the order of rule, was David's age, over land, over earth, a dwelling of grace [?], when he took true sovereignty.
Of David, without strife then, the wise ones of the histories tell that for forty strong years his rule was governed.
Four champions [?], just was their destruction, fell by David: Ishbi-benob [?], Saph [?], fair Goliath, and the man with six fingers.
Four who composed [?] a bright lay with David son of Jesse: shapely Ethan, of mysterious wishes, Asaph, Heman, Jeduthun.
Ahithophel, a turning without attack [?], and Hushai the Archite, two with high [?] peace, were the chief counsellors of David.
When David took the high leadership, of fiery [?] and certain fierceness, in dreadful battle, above every fame [?], he was fully thirty. Thirty years, without folly of strength.
There was built by him, a festival without sorrow, the chief city of the sons of Israel; on Mount Zion, with ranks of [?], he founded Jerusalem.
He set it on the mountain, a sound seat, fair [?] Zion, with ranks of noble grades; he established [?] it towards the east above the hill, a fitting city with a forked [?] point.
Thirty thousand warriors, a deed without fault, went with David to fetch the ark with honour from the house of Abinadab.
With choirs of clear songs, with harps of pleasant music, with organs fairer than bands of singers, with treasures, with great honours.
The ark was on a cart [?] of pledge [?] while being brought to Jerusalem: Uzzah put his hand on the pure ark: Uzzah was dead at once.
When he raised it, a kingly company [?], with the hosts of Jerusalem, the ark of God [?] over every foot [?] was brought by him to the chief city.
Before the holy ark, the glory of a chief [?], with very great joy, David would leap with agility, with ranks of rule [?], like a fool at buffoonery.
It was angrily [?] that proud, high-spirited Michal looked out upon the king, a course without restraint [?]; his nakedness was plain to her.
She reproached the king with rancour [?] and roused him to great anger, so that David, a harsh sound, laid his curse upon Michal.
The city without firm breaking [?], whose name is Jerusalem, a fair building, fame took hold of it; above every place it was raised. It was built by him, a festival without sorrow.
David, with [?] of towers, for a time over the [?] land of Jerusalem, ruled under a form of grace for thirty-three certain years.
The strong lord arranged a [?] assembly after the building of Jerusalem, over every bold host [?], a strong throng, in the full kingdom of Israel.
Mephibosheth, for noble protection [?], the lame son who was Jonathan's: David raised him above the throngs, beyond everyone, into his lifelong companionship.
Amnon son of David, a famous deed: he used force on Tamar. Between man and woman there is danger; from this came his destruction.
Absalom, who was not peaceable [?], killed Amnon son of David, so that he was ... [?] under attack [?] in exile for three years.
Once David's people, a peaceful company [?], went to the king of Ammon; their tunics were cut around them and half their beards were shaved.
David, of perfect fame, did not let them make a hasty return to the great host; they stayed in Jericho to recover and to ... [?].
David brought Hanun son of Nahash, king of Ammon, to his final death, and took from his rightful head the crown that held a talent of red gold.
David, with clear raids [?], plundered the land of Ammon on every side; Rabbah, the city of the Ammonites, was subdued by swarms of troops.
For three years, of poor strength, there was famine in the time of David, so that all were in danger of death on account of the Ammonites.
Saul broke a firm covenant with the Ammonites in Israel; he put them under harsh bondage [?] and killed a host of the Ammonites.
The angel of God, who brings every peace [?], said clearly to David: so that vengeance should not fall on the host, it should be exacted from the [offspring] of Saul.
Seven men of Saul's offspring were given up on behalf of the host; David handed them over ... [?] into the hands of the Ammonites.
By the Ammonites, according to a covenant, to fulfil the covenant, by God's will (famous is the lore), they were crucified on one hill.
Shammua [?], Shobab, noble Nathan, Solomon and Ibhar, Elishua, full of beauty every day, Nepheg [?] and Japhia.
Elishama (a lofty saying), Eliada, Eliphelet [?]: the children of David, rows of ... [?]; they were born to him in Jerusalem.
A king with whom the bright world ... [?], a king with very great ... [?], a king with swift blades of ... [?]: David rose up from among the peoples. David with fierce ... [?].
The Syrians gathered firm assemblies of warlike hosts, with strong, mighty ... [?], to destroy the sons of Israel.
To destroy the people swiftly, to lay waste from them as far as Africa [?], with the invasion of the lords, a mighty tumult, to destroy Jerusalem.
They had truly vowed that once they went into the land of Egypt, they would never come back to their homes until they had plundered Alexandria.
David, sure in knowledge [?], fought them; the red-speared one drove them under ... [?], so that the battlefields were full of them from red streams [of blood].
David, of comely face, slew of them ten thousand foot soldiers for certain, eight hundred fitted hard chariots, and forty thousand horsemen.
The king who surpassed every king, a king without danger, without weakness: the strong king David, sure in his portion, put them to ... [?] rout.
The host of the Syrians, ranks of throngs, ... [?] excellent, of sharp-edged deeds, broad, swift, ... [?], fierce peoples: they gathered. They gathered firm assemblies.
He overcame the swift peoples and put them all under fear [?]; through the raging fury of mighty-handed deeds [?] a ... [?] of pride filled him.
David overran many lands round about, fierce and harsh, under fair kingship; David, though he was a godly chief, committed much transgression.
When he had counted the number of the host that was under his power, of great clans [?]; when he took the woman whom he ... [?]; when he killed her mighty warrior.

With gifts, with tributes [?], with great quantities of strongholds [?], with treasures, with thousands of great diadems: clearly he ended [?] through the terror he caused and through his battles, and he brought them under his feet to subdue them. He subdued the fierce peoples. [Canto] 120
When Joab was sent (it was a sad tale) to count the host of the sons of Israel, from Dan, [?] of God, to the plain [?] of the land of Beersheba,
nine full months (a swift company) and twenty days less one, for a long stretch, the mighty lords, until they reached Jerusalem.
Joab made the count of the host for the noble king in the royal assembly. He reported rightly (the love of dear God) thirteen hundred thousand of them.
Eight hundred thousand under one law of the people of the eleven tribes; the tribe of Judah, truly, the tale relates, five hundred thousand very strong men.
After each count of them that he found, with full [?] against victorious [?], he then said, a cry without sorrow: "May God increase the host of Israel."
"Had noble Joab not blessed them," said the pure, very modest angel, "the wrath of God would have been woven upon [?] both king and people."

Joab was perfect in righteous deeds toward the king and toward the host, whom he loved greatly. From land to land, with forceful judgment, he was sent by the king to count them. When Joab was sent, it was a sad tale.
The Lord was angry with him, a complete burden [?], for the counting of the great hosts, since it was not he in any way who fed them or clothed them.
Dear God, the Lord of holy heaven, had another anger, since he had slain his soldier (great valour) and taken his wife after killing him.
The Spirit of God spoke to Gad a clear, final, complete message: "Say to David (it is no lie) that he has a choice among three judgments:
"seven years of lasting poverty for him, and famine with its wandering [?]; or three months of being driven before the raiding of his enemies; or a blaze of disease for three days."
Gad spoke to David then, though it saddened his mind: "Vengeance will come, O lord [?], for your proud thought."
After that, David asked to be spared from falling into the hands of his enemies; whatever vengeance He himself thought best, let Him bring it upon them by His pure will.

He was routed and found no refuge before Joab and David's people, until he reached the city of a hundred [?], Abel-beth-maacah.

From the wall, before the host outside, she called out to the son of Zeruiah (it was a perfect deed, not a sad one [?]), and so drew Joab to speak with her.

David enjoyed his dignity and his sovereignty without hindrance, until after that he left the full kingship whole to Solomon.
Shimei son of Gera, [?] after his quarrel with David, quickly bowed down to David across the Jordan when he came. When David came from the south.

With perfect wisdom and pure form, Solomon's knowledge surpassed every host: there was testimony enough from every plain to his dignity and his honour.
The wisdom of Solomon, with ranks of hosts, was famous above the world, great as red gold. Solomon's like, in pure peace, was not found among the kings of the earth.
Solomon had twelve sub-kings, of eager voice. Each one, in his turn (a sure tale), was over the twelve tribes of Israel.

Solomon ruled above kings in wisdom and great dignity. He answered the challenges of true hosts, and he was most wonderful in powers and in bursts of valour. Solomon ruled, with ranks of hosts.
By him the building was raised from the ground, bounded and complete, above every famous plain and of pure form: Solomon's venerable and beautiful temple.
David leaves two [?] for Solomon to put to death: mighty Joab ... who proclaimed battle, and Shimei son of Gera.

Son of David, of strong benefit, wonderful king of Israel's son [?], without falsehood, without taboo, with fortunes of building [?]: by Solomon the temple was raised. By him it was raised from the ground.

Solomon, who was a sage whom throngs sought out to learn great wisdom, parted from victory and from fame from the time he worshipped the idols. From the worship of the splendid idols.
The King, with a full clamour [?], brought vengeance on the illustrious king Jeroboam when the prophet rebuked him in particular while he was worshipping the idol.

The King of the world, a power that does not lie, who [?] of pure branches, who fashioned [?] every king under the bright sun: he is the King who brought the vengeance. The King brought vengeance, with a full clamour [?].

A King whom Simeon praised, as was fitting, when he was at the pure altar, when he raised upon his own hand the high King of heaven, holy and noble.
A King who laid a strong command upon the wondrous stream of the Jordan, so that it did not move (fame without restriction) while he was at his baptism.
A King who stood before the hosts, a great King, truly good, fair and great, upon whom the Holy Spirit settled, with the speech of the truly noble Lord.
Son of God, divine God both; he was one, he was threefold, surely pure; he was not proud in his speech, a most victorious King who was born. A King was born, without sin.
